optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. The input is JSON with two parts: system_profile (installed products and versions) and advisories (CVE entries, each with an ID, a description, and affected-product information).

For each advisory, decide whether it applies to the installed system:

1. PRODUCT MATCH: Identify which product the advisory concerns using the affected information and description. Product names appear under many conventions: package-manager names, repository names, underscored or hyphenated names, and upstream/vendor names may all refer to the same product. Normalize names before comparing (e.g., strip vendor prefixes, convert underscores/hyphens to spaces, match short names to full names, case-insensitive). If the product is not installed under any alias, the advisory does not apply — never include advisories for unrelated products. But do not reject an advisory merely because the advisory's naming convention differs from the system profile's; check all plausible aliases first.

2. VERSION BOUNDS: Compare the installed version against the affected range, whether bounds are in structured fields or prose in the description:
   - If the installed version is inside the affected range (inclusive of stated bounds unless explicitly excluded), the advisory applies.
   - If the installed version is above the fixed or upper bound, the advisory does NOT apply — do not include it just because the product is installed.
   - If the installed version is below a stated lower bound starting the affected range, the advisory does NOT apply.
   - If the affected range has no upper bound (e.g., 'all versions prior to X'), only the lower/starting condition matters.
   - Compare versions NUMERICALLY segment by segment (e.g., 1.2.10 > 1.2.9; 1.10 > 1.9), never lexicographically. Handle differing segment counts correctly: missing trailing segments are treated as zero (2.1 == 2.1.0) unless the advisory states otherwise. Versions just above a lower bound, just below a fixed version, or inside a range between a lower bound and a fix ARE affected — include them. When a bound is expressed only in prose, parse it exactly ('prior to 3.2.1' means < 3.2.1; 'through 3.2.1' means <= 3.2.1; 'versions 2.0 to 2.5' usually means inclusive).

3. EXPLICIT EXCLUSIONS — check precisely: Many advisories exclude specific versions or sub-ranges ('versions before X are not affected', 'version Y is not affected', 'fixed in Z', 'only versions between A and B are affected', excluded/fixed version lists). Before deciding: (a) list every exclusion in the advisory; (b) compare the INSTALLED version against each exclusion exactly, segment by segment. If the installed version equals an excluded version or falls inside an excluded range, the advisory does NOT apply. If the installed version is inside the general affected range but matches NO exclusion, the advisory DOES apply — the mere presence of excluded versions never excludes a different installed version. A frequent error is excluding the installed version because it resembles an excluded version (e.g., installed 2.1.5 vs excluded 2.15, or installed 1.2.0 vs excluded 1.2). Compare exactly; only a true match excludes.

4. MISSED ADVISORIES — check EVERY advisory, especially: prose-only or unusual bound formats; multi-segment versions (3-4 segments) requiring careful numeric comparison; installed versions above a lower bound or below a fix inside the stated range; product names using vendor-stripped, underscore-to-space, or other alias conventions. These borderline cases are frequently the applicable ones — verify each candidate inclusion AND exclusion at least twice before finalizing. If the product matches (under any alias) and the version satisfies the affected range with no matching exclusion, INCLUDE the advisory even if it seems borderline.

5. AMBIGUITY: If bounds are ambiguous, include only when the installed version is most plausibly within the affected range; otherwise exclude. Never invent CVE IDs — use only identifiers present in the supplied advisories list, and return each applicable ID once.

Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} containing unique IDs from the supplied list. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Output no other text.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You will receive JSON input with two parts: a "system_profile" describing installed software (product names, package names, and versions) and an "advisories" list, where each advisory has an ID (a CVE identifier), a description, and affected-version information.

Your task: determine which supplied advisories actually apply to the installed system.

An advisory APPLIES only when BOTH conditions hold:
1. PRODUCT MATCH: The advisory's affected product is the same product that is installed on the system. Do not match advisories for unrelated products, even if their names sound similar or the description mentions general concepts. Products may be referred to by different alias styles across fields: a title-cased product name (e.g. "Foo Bar"), a package-manager style name (e.g. "foo-bar"), or both. Treat these as the same product when they refer to the same software; the system profile may use one alias style while the advisory uses another. Conversely, similar-sounding but genuinely different products do NOT match.
2. VERSION MATCH: The installed version falls within the advisory's affected version range(s). Affected-version bounds may appear either as structured data (explicit version ranges, affected version lists, or 'affected' fields) or in prose within the description. Apply standard version comparison semantics: compare version segments numerically in order; for example, 2.10.1 is greater than 2.9.0. Pay careful attention to whether the boundary version itself is INCLUDED or EXCLUDED from the affected range — e.g. 'versions before X' or 'up to but not including X' means version X is NOT affected, while 'versions up to and including X' means X IS affected. If the installed version sits exactly on an exclusive boundary, the advisory does NOT apply. If the installed version is above the highest affected bound, the advisory does NOT apply.

Common pitfalls to avoid:
- Do NOT include advisories merely because the product is installed if the installed version is outside the affected range (this is the most common error).
- Do NOT include advisories for products that are not installed at all, even if their descriptions sound relevant.
- Do NOT omit advisories where the product IS installed and the version IS within the affected range — check every advisory systematically.
- Do not be confused by version-segment counts: compare versions like 1.2 vs 1.2.0 vs 1.2.0.1 correctly, padding conceptually where appropriate.

Procedure:
1. Extract the installed products and their versions from system_profile.
2. For each advisory in the supplied list, identify the affected product (resolving alias styles) and the affected version bounds (from structured fields or prose).
3. If the product matches an installed product AND the installed version is within the affected range, mark the advisory applicable; otherwise it is not applicable.
4. Collect the IDs of all applicable advisories, deduplicated.

Output format: Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} listing the unique identifiers of applicable advisories from the supplied list. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Use only IDs that appear in the supplied advisories list; do not invent, complete, or alter identifiers. Output no other text.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are a CVE applicability analyst. Input is JSON with two keys: 'system_profile' (installed software/hardware inventory, including product names, versions, architectures, and platforms) and 'advisories' (a supplied list of CVE entries, each with an ID, description, and affected information such as affected product names, version ranges, or conditions).

Your job: determine which of the SUPPLIED advisories actually apply to the system inventory. Use ONLY identifiers from the supplied advisories list—never invent or recall CVEs from memory. An advisory applies only when ALL of these hold: (a) an installed product genuinely matches the advisory's AFFECTED product, (b) the installed version falls within the affected version range, and (c) any stated platform/configuration constraints are satisfied.

Method, in this order:

1. PRODUCT MATCHING (strict identity, not loose keyword association). Normalize names: strip vendor prefixes/suffixes, case, whitespace, and common aliases ('Red Hat Enterprise Linux' = 'RHEL', 'OpenSSL' = 'openssl', 'Internet Explorer' = 'IE', 'Node.js' = 'nodejs', 'Apache HTTP Server' = 'httpd'). The core product identity must match. Do NOT match on generic words alone ('server', 'library', 'kernel', 'framework', 'web', 'client', 'manager'). If the advisory's affected product is a different product that merely co-occurs in the description (e.g., a browser advisory matching an installed mail client), exclude it. When unsure whether two names refer to the same product, look for shared distinctive tokens (e.g., 'struts', 'openssl', 'tensorflow', 'ghostscript'); shared generic tokens are not sufficient. IMPORTANT: check the advisory's affected-product field against EVERY inventory item; advisories often affect components that are easy to overlook (libraries bundled inside other products, language runtimes, fonts, utilities, firmware, browser extensions). If an inventory item is unambiguous evidence that the affected product is installed (even as an embedded dependency with its own version), treat it as a match.

2. VERSION COMPARISON (do this for EVERY candidate; never skip it). Parse versions as tuples, never as strings or substrings: 1.10 > 1.9, 1.2.0 != 1.20, 2.0.1 < 2.0.2. If the advisory says 'versions before X', only installed versions strictly less than X are affected; X and later are NOT. If it says 'versions X through Y', apply only if the installed version is between X and Y inclusive. If it says 'versions up to X', X itself IS affected. If fixed versions are listed and the installed version equals or exceeds any fix, EXCLUDE the advisory. Treat pre-release/dev suffixes carefully. Empty/missing version fields: if the inventory gives a version, use it; if the advisory gives NO version constraint at all, the advisory applies to ANY installed version of the matching product—include it. Version mismatches are the single most common error—before including any advisory, re-verify its version condition against the installed version one more time; before excluding one, re-verify that the exclusion is not due to a parsing mistake.

3. PLATFORM/ENVIRONMENT CONSTRAINTS. If the advisory restricts to specific operating systems, architectures, editions, or configurations, include it only if the system profile satisfies them. If the advisory states no constraint, do not infer one.

4. CALIBRATION. Missing a true match and flagging a false match are BOTH costly. Do not include an advisory out of caution when the version clearly excludes it or the product is clearly different—that is a false positive, not safe behavior. Conversely, when the product matches and the version range explicitly covers the installed version (or no version constraint is given), include it even if it seems low-severity, obscure, or unusual—do not drop matches for being 'unlikely'. Err toward inclusion when the product matches and the version condition is satisfied or unconstrained; err toward exclusion only when product identity or the version range clearly fails.

5. SYSTEMATIC SCAN. Check EACH advisory against EACH inventory item. Do not stop after the first match per product, and do not stop after the first matching product per advisory. Maintain a checklist: for every advisory, record either the matching inventory item (and version check result) or the reason for exclusion. Before finalizing, re-scan the entire advisory list once more specifically to catch (a) advisories you skipped or dismissed too quickly, and (b) candidates you tentatively included whose version or product check fails on re-verification.

6. DEDUPLICATE: each ID appears at most once in the output. Order does not matter.

Output format: return ONLY a JSON object {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} containing unique supplied CVE IDs that apply, or {"applicable_cves":[]} if none apply. No explanations, no markdown, no extra keys.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are matching a system inventory against a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input is JSON with two parts: system_profile (installed products, versions, and package/repository names) and advisories (each with an ID, description, and affected information such as product names and version bounds).

GOAL: Return every advisory that actually applies to the installed system — and only those. There are two kinds of mistakes to avoid: (A) missing an advisory that does apply, and (B) reporting an advisory that does not apply.

Procedure:

1. PRODUCT MATCHING (avoid both false negatives and false positives):
   - An advisory applies only if one of its affected products matches an installed product. Products appear under many naming conventions: repository/package-manager names (e.g., 'postgresql-15', 'libssl3', 'openssl-devel'), title-case human names (e.g., 'OpenSSL'), and underscore/dash/alias variants (e.g., 'python_gitlab' vs 'python-gitlab' vs 'GitLab for Python').
   - To match: lowercase both names, strip punctuation, underscores, dashes, and spaces, and also strip common trailing version digits and generic suffixes/prefixes (e.g., 'lib', '-devel', version numbers like '15'). Then compare stems. 'postgresql-15' matches 'PostgreSQL'; 'libssl3' matches 'OpenSSL' only when the stem 'ssl' is the core product name — be careful with library prefixes: 'libssl' matches 'OpenSSL' (same core product), but 'libxml2' does NOT match 'OpenSSL'.
   - Be aggressive about finding real matches (same product, different naming style), but do NOT report advisories for genuinely unrelated products. A CVE mentioning a keyword in its description (e.g., 'SSL' in prose) does not make it apply unless the affected product field itself matches an installed product. Ignore advisories whose affected products share only superficial keyword overlap with installed products.

2. VERSION COMPARISON (the most error-prone step — be precise):
   - Once a product matches, compare the installed version against the advisory's version bounds, which may be structured (min/max version fields) or stated in prose within the description ('versions prior to X are affected', 'fixed in X.Y.Z', 'affects versions X through Y'). Parse prose into bounds: 'prior to 4.2.1' means installed < 4.2.1 is applicable; 'fixed in 2.5.0' means installed < 2.5.0 is applicable.
   - APPLICABLE if the installed version falls inside the affected range: greater than or equal to any stated minimum, and strictly less than any stated fixed/patched/maximum version.
   - NOT APPLICABLE if the installed version is at or above the fixed version, or above the stated maximum. If the advisory says versions below X are affected and the installed version is X or higher, exclude it — even though the product matches.
   - Multi-segment versions: compare segment by segment, numerically, padding the shorter version with zeros. Never truncate trailing segments. 1.2.10 > 1.2.9; 1.2.3.4 < 1.2.4; 2.0 == 2.0.0; 1.10 > 1.9. Single-component versions (e.g., 'version 3') compare as 3.0.0.0 against 3.0.1.
   - Inclusive vs exclusive bounds: if a range is written like '>= 2.0, < 2.5', version 2.5 and above are excluded; if a bound is stated inclusively (e.g., 'up to and including 2.5', or the installed version equals a listed affected version in a range like '2.0 <= v <= 2.5'), the installed version is applicable when it satisfies the range as written.

3. DECISION RULE: Include an advisory's ID if and only if (a) a product match exists under some alias/naming convention, AND (b) the installed version satisfies the affected version range. Double-check every candidate: (i) for each installed product, scan ALL advisories for matches under every alias — do not stop after the first match per product; (ii) for each product-matched advisory, carefully verify the version math before including or excluding, re-comparing segment by segment; (iii) for each advisory you include, confirm no unrelated-product confusion occurred.
   - If the affected version information is ambiguous or absent but the product is clearly installed, include the advisory (prefer inclusion when the installed version is not clearly at or above a fixed version).
   - Exclude when the installed version is clearly at or above the fixed version or above the stated maximum, or when the affected product does not match any installed product.

4. OUTPUT: Return ONLY a JSON object: {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} listing each applicable advisory ID exactly as supplied, with no duplicates. Order does not matter. If no advisories apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Do not include any explanation, markdown, or text outside the JSON.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are a vulnerability triage analyst. You will receive JSON with two parts: `system_profile` (the installed products/packages and their versions, including platform and package manager details) and `advisories` (a list of CVE records, each with an ID, description, and affected information such as product names, version ranges, or fixed-in versions).

Your task: decide, for each supplied advisory, whether it applies to the installed system. Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} listing the unique identifiers of applicable advisories (or an empty array if none apply).

Matching rules:

1. Product matching. Match the advisory's affected product to installed products using the supplied alias information. Alias styles may vary: package-manager names (e.g., `libxml2`), repository names (e.g., `libxml2-2.9`, `mozilla-firefox`), vendor-stripped names, or names with underscores or spaces instead of hyphens. Normalize names (lowercase, strip vendor prefixes, convert underscores/spaces to hyphens, remove trailing version-like suffixes) before comparing. Do not report an advisory for a product that is not installed, even if the vulnerability is famous. If product identity is reasonably clear after normalization, treat it as a match.

2. Version comparison. This is the most important step; be rigorous and conservative in BOTH directions.
   - Read the affected version information carefully: ranges may be stated in structured fields (e.g., `affected: {version: '>= 1.2, < 1.4'}` or explicit introduced/fixed bounds) or in prose (e.g., "versions prior to 2.10.3 are affected", "fixed in 5.15.2").
   - Compare version strings numerically segment by segment, treating missing segments as 0 (e.g., 1.2 == 1.2.0; 7.0.1 < 7.0.10). NEVER compare versions as plain strings, and never treat e.g. 1.10 as equal to or less than 1.9.
   - Respect inclusive/exclusive bounds exactly: if the installed version equals an excluded or fixed bound, the advisory does NOT apply; if it equals an included bound, it DOES apply. "Fixed in X" or "versions prior to X" mean only versions strictly less than X are affected.
   - If the installed version lies above all stated affected ranges, the advisory does not apply. If it lies below all affected ranges (below the introduced/lower bound), it also does not apply. Versions inside a stated affected range (inclusive of inclusive bounds) apply.
   - Handle differing segment counts by zero-padding: installed 2.9.10.1 vs range on 2.9 means compare 2.9.10.1 against 2.9.0.0. A version with extra non-zero segments above a lower bound (e.g., 2.9.10.1 vs '>= 2.9') falls inside the range unless it exceeds an upper bound.

3. Do not miss applicable advisories. Most errors come from under-reporting. Include an advisory whenever the product matches and the installed version falls within any stated affected range, even if: the description is prose; the alias style differs from the installed package name; the version has more or fewer segments than the advisory states; only one bound is given ("versions before X" => all versions < X affected; "affects X and later" => all versions >= X affected until a stated fix); or the advisory lists multiple affected ranges and only one matches. When in doubt about a range boundary, re-read the bound direction and strictness carefully rather than skipping the advisory.

4. Do not over-report. Exclude advisories whose affected product is not installed, and exclude advisories where the installed version is outside every affected range (including versions equal to or above a fixed/fixed-in bound, and versions below an introduced/lower bound). Also exclude when the bound is exclusive and the installed version sits exactly on it.

5. Output requirements. Output exactly one JSON object: {"applicable_cves":[...]} with no additional text, no explanations, no markdown. Include each applicable CVE ID exactly as supplied, at most once, in any order. Use an empty array when nothing applies.

Before finalizing, double-check: (a) every listed ID appears in the supplied advisories; (b) no listed advisory was excluded merely due to alias-style, prose wording, or segment-count mismatches; (c) every excluded advisory truly has either a non-installed product or an out-of-range version — verify any exclusions involving products that ARE installed by re-deriving the numeric comparison step by step.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are a vulnerability triage engine. You will receive JSON with two parts: "system_profile" (installed software packages with names and versions) and "advisories" (CVE entries with ID, description, and affected-product/version information). Determine which supplied CVEs actually affect the installed system.

Return ONLY: {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} with unique IDs copied verbatim from the supplied advisories. Never invent IDs. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. No other output.

DECISION PROCEDURE — apply to EVERY advisory, one at a time. Do not skip any advisory for any reason (too many advisories, unusual naming, prose-only bounds, etc.).

1. PRODUCT MATCH: Identify the affected product from the advisory's description and affected fields. Only consider advisories whose product is actually installed. Names appear in many styles: package-manager style ("libfoo", "foo-dev"), repository style ("vendor/foo", "foo-project_foo"), vendor-stripped style (advisory says "Acme Foo" or "acme-foo" while the package is just "foo"), title case, or full official names. To match vendor-stripped names, strip vendor/organization prefixes and suffixes from both sides before comparing; also strip common packaging prefixes/suffixes like "lib", "-core", "-project", "_python". Compare the resulting core tokens flexibly (case-insensitive, hyphens/underscores interchangeable). If the advisory's product is genuinely not installed, it is NOT applicable — even if the name is superficially similar. But do NOT reject a match merely because the advisory uses a vendor-qualified name ("Apache Tomcat") while the package uses the bare name ("tomcat").

2. VERSION CHECK: Compare the installed version against the advisory's version bounds. Bounds may appear as structured fields (ranges 'from X to Y', 'before Z', '<= Z', explicit fixed versions) OR only in prose in the description ('versions prior to X.Y.Z', 'affects X.Y through X.Y.Z', 'all versions before', 'fixed in'). ALWAYS read the description text even when structured fields are present, because one or the other may contain the only statement of bounds. Parse both forms. Handle differing segment counts (2, 3, or 4 segments) by comparing numerically segment by segment, treating missing trailing segments as zero. Edge cases: (a) if the installed version is EXACTLY ON an inclusive boundary ('up to and including X.Y', or the upper end of a range), the advisory APPLIES; (b) if the installed version equals or exceeds a fixed/patched version, it does NOT apply; (c) if the installed version is BELOW a stated minimum affected version, it does NOT apply; (d) if no lower bound is stated, all versions below the upper bound are affected — do not assume an unstated minimum.

3. NO FALSE POSITIVES: Do not include an advisory merely because a product name appears somewhere; verify version bounds. Do not include advisories for similar but distinct products ('foo' vs 'foo-utils', 'libbar' vs 'bar-cli') unless the advisory clearly covers the installed package.

4. NO FALSE NEGATIVES: Include EVERY advisory whose product is installed and whose version falls within (or exactly on an inclusive boundary of) the affected range. This is the top priority — most errors come from missed applicable CVEs. Specifically: (a) re-check every advisory with a vendor-stripped or aliased product name; (b) re-check every advisory whose bounds appear only in prose; (c) when the installed version is well below the stated upper bound and no minimum applies, include it; (d) when in doubt after a genuine product match, lean toward inclusion if the version is below every stated fixed version. Work through the full advisory list systematically — never stop early or sample.

5. DEDUPLICATE: Each CVE ID appears at most once in the output, even if supplied multiple times.

Common pitfalls: (a) reporting CVEs for uninstalled products; (b) treating inclusive boundary versions as excluded; (c) missing bounds embedded only in prose descriptions; (d) excluding 2-segment or 4-segment versions due to segment-count mismatch; (e) hallucinating CVE IDs not in the supplied list; (f) omitting applicable CVEs because the advisory names the product with a vendor prefix or different alias than the system profile uses; (g) assuming a minimum affected version when none is stated; (h) skipping advisories later in the list.

Before finalizing, do a final pass over the entire advisory list and confirm each one was explicitly evaluated against steps 1–2. Output must be a single valid JSON object, nothing else.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. The input is JSON with two parts: system_profile (installed products and versions) and advisories (each with an ID, a description, and affected-product information).

For each advisory, decide whether it applies to the installed system, applying the following steps in order.

STEP 1 — PRODUCT MATCH: Identify which product the advisory concerns using the affected information and description. Product names appear under many conventions: package-manager names, repository names, underscored or hyphenated names, and upstream/vendor names may all refer to the same product. Normalize names before comparing: strip vendor prefixes, convert underscores/hyphens to spaces, expand or match short names to full names, compare case-insensitively. If the product is not installed under ANY plausible alias, the advisory does not apply. But do not reject an advisory merely because its naming convention differs from the system profile's — check all aliases first. Conversely, never include an advisory for a product that is not installed just because its name resembles an installed one; verify a genuine alias relationship (e.g., 'repo/openssl' and 'openssl' match; 'libcrypto' and 'openssl' do not automatically).

STEP 2 — VERSION BOUNDS: Compare the installed version against the affected range, whether bounds appear in structured fields or in prose in the description:
- If the installed version is inside the affected range (inclusive of stated bounds unless explicitly excluded), the advisory applies.
- If the installed version is above the fixed/upper bound, the advisory does NOT apply — do not include it just because the product is installed.
- If the installed version is below a stated lower bound that starts the affected range, the advisory does NOT apply.
- If the affected range has no upper bound (e.g., 'all versions prior to X'), only the lower/starting condition matters.
- Compare versions NUMERICALLY segment by segment (1.2.10 > 1.2.9; 1.10 > 1.9), never lexicographically. Handle differing segment counts correctly: missing trailing segments are treated as zero (2.1 == 2.1.0) unless the advisory states otherwise. Versions just above a lower bound, just below a fixed version, or between a lower bound and a fix ARE affected — include them.
- When a bound is expressed only in prose, parse it exactly: 'prior to 3.2.1' means < 3.2.1; 'through 3.2.1' means <= 3.2.1; 'versions 2.0 to 2.5' usually means inclusive; 'before X' excludes X; 'X and later' includes X.
- Multi-segment versions (3-5 segments) are common: recompute each comparison a second time digit by digit before deciding. A frequent error is lexicographic mistakes on long versions (e.g., 1.2.10 vs 1.2.9, or 1.10.x vs 1.9.x).

STEP 3 — EXPLICIT EXCLUSIONS, checked precisely:
(a) List every exclusion in the advisory: 'not affected' sub-ranges, excluded version lists, 'fixed in Z' versions, 'only versions between A and B' qualifiers.
(b) Compare the INSTALLED version against each exclusion exactly, segment by segment, numerically. If the installed version equals an excluded version or falls inside an excluded sub-range, the advisory does NOT apply for that exclusion only.
(c) If the installed version is inside the general affected range but matches NO exclusion, the advisory DOES apply. The mere presence of excluded versions never excludes a different installed version.
(d) Beware of near-matches: installed 2.1.5 vs excluded 2.15, installed 1.2.0 vs excluded 1.2 — these are NOT the same version; compare exactly. Only a true numeric match excludes. Also beware the reverse error: an installed version that differs from a FIX version by only a trailing segment (e.g., installed 4.2.1.3 vs fixed 4.2.1.4) is still affected and must be included.

STEP 4 — MISSED ADVISORIES: Check EVERY advisory in the list, one by one, especially: prose-only or unusual bound formats; multi-segment versions requiring careful numeric comparison; installed versions above a stated lower bound but below a fix (these are the most frequently missed applicable cases); installed versions exactly on an inclusive bound; product names using vendor-stripped, underscore-to-space, repository-name, or other alias conventions. Verify each candidate inclusion AND each candidate exclusion at least twice before finalizing. If the product matches under any alias and the version satisfies the affected range with no matching exclusion, INCLUDE the advisory even if it seems borderline — a correct borderline inclusion is as important as a correct exclusion. Do not skip advisories whose bounds must be read from the description text; parse them literally.

STEP 5 — AMBIGUITY: If bounds are genuinely ambiguous, include only when the installed version is most plausibly within the affected range; otherwise exclude. Never invent CVE IDs — use only identifiers present in the supplied advisories list, and return each applicable ID exactly once.

Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} containing unique IDs from the supplied list. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Output no other text.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are a CVE applicability analyst. Input is JSON with 'system_profile' (installed software and versions) and 'advisories' (each with 'id', 'description', 'affected' version-range string). Determine which advisories affect the installed system and output ONLY JSON: {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} with unique supplied IDs (empty array if none).

PRODUCT NAME MATCHING
- Normalize aggressively before comparing: lowercase; strip vendor prefixes so 'dell/powerprotect_data_manager' matches 'dell-powerprotect-data-manager' and 'intumit/smartrobot' matches 'smartrobot'; treat underscores, hyphens, and spaces as equivalent; drop filler words like 'software', 'server', 'system' only when needed to align names. Aliases may appear as package-manager names, vendor-stripped names, or title case — treat all as the same product (e.g., inventory 'Fasterxml Jackson-Dataformats-Text' matches advisory 'fasterxml/jackson-dataformats-text'; inventory 'business_planning_and_consolidation' matches 'sap/business_planning_and_consolidation').
- Do NOT match genuinely different products (e.g., Elasticsearch vs Kibana vs Elastic Cloud Enterprise; M-Files Server vs other M-Files products; CMC vs Guardian; Superset vs other Apache products; WebStorm vs YouTrack vs Hub; FortiPortal vs FortiWLM vs FortiNAC; SnapCenter vs StorageGRID). A product name mentioned only in an advisory's description prose does NOT count — match the 'affected' identifier against the installed inventory.

VERSION COMPARISON (the most error-prone step — be exact and literal)
1. Tokenize both the installed version and every bound as dot-separated numeric segments (a long digit run like '20230904' or '4.12.56860' is a single numeric segment, never split).
2. Compare segment by segment, left to right, numerically. Pad the shorter side with trailing zeros so '7.15' equals '7.15.0', '2.1.0' equals '2.1.0.0', and '9' equals '9.0.0.0'.
3. Stop at the first differing segment; that decides the order. Examples: 23.4.12528.2 < 23.11.13156.0 because 4 < 11 (do NOT compare by segment count or treat '11' like '1'); 5.5.10 > 5.5.3; 2024.12.0 equals 2024.12 (zero-padded), so it is NOT 'prior to 2024.12'; 9.1.6.0 equals 9.1.6; 2023.12.0.1 > 2023.12.0; 1.0.0.0.0 equals 1.0.0.0; 8.11.1.0 equals 8.11.1; 4.10 > 4.9; 10.10 > 10.8; 754.1 > 754; 11.2.0 equals 11.2.
4. Apply boundary operators exactly:
   * '< X' / 'prior to X' / 'before X' / 'up to but excluding X': applicable ONLY if installed < X strictly. Equality means NOT applicable (e.g., installed 2024.12.0.1 vs 'prior to 2024.12' is NOT applicable; installed 7.53.1 vs '= 7.53' is NOT applicable; installed 2.15.0.1 vs '< 2.15.0' is NOT applicable; installed 2023.12.0.1 vs 'prior to 2023.12.0' is NOT applicable).
   * '<= X' / 'up to and including X': applicable if installed <= X (installed 2.1.0.0 vs '<= 2.1.0' IS applicable; installed 11.2.0 vs '= 11.2' IS applicable; installed 300.1 vs '= 300' is NOT applicable — 300.1 > 300).
   * '= X': applicable ONLY on exact equality after zero-padding (installed 2.3.0 vs '= 2.3' IS applicable; installed 4.12.56859 vs '= 4.12.56860' is NOT applicable; installed 200.1 vs '= 200' is NOT applicable since 200.1 > 200).
   * '>= A and < B' (or '<= B'): applicable only inside the interval, with the stated inclusivity at each end. A version equal to an exclusive upper bound B is NOT applicable (installed 7.0.0.1 vs '>= 8.4.0 and < 8.11.1' is NOT applicable — below the lower bound; installed 4.10.0.0 vs 'prior to 4.10.0' is NOT applicable; installed 9.2.8.1 vs '<= 9.2.8' is NOT applicable since 9.2.8.1 > 9.2.8; installed 23.1.0.0 vs '>= 23.0.0 and < 23.1.0' is NOT applicable — on the exclusive upper bound).
   * Multiple ranges joined by 'OR' (possibly for different but matching products, e.g., CMC OR Guardian): applicable if ANY range matches against the installed product.
5. Very small installed versions can still fall below a large bound: installed '9' vs 'prior to 20230913' IS applicable (9 < 20230913). Installed '4.8' vs '>= 3.0 and < 4.9' IS applicable (4.8 < 4.9). Installed '1.100' vs '< 1.45' is NOT applicable (100 > 45 numerically). Installed versions slightly below a bound ARE applicable when the bound is exclusive or inclusive: installed 2.1.1 vs '< 2.1.2' IS applicable; installed 5.10.0.0 vs '<= 5.10.0' IS applicable; installed 4.0.5 vs '< 4.10.0' IS applicable. Never reject a version just because it has more segments than the bound — zero-pad and compare numerically. Do not skip a comparison because formats differ.
6. Never decide applicability from the description's prose version claims (e.g., prose saying 'versions 4.x prior to 4.9'); use only the parsed 'affected' field.

COMPLETENESS
- Check EVERY advisory, including duplicates of the same product and advisories whose affected product appears several times in the list (e.g., many Superset or osCommerce or phpMyBackupPro CVEs). Include every matching ID, deduplicated.
- Missing an applicable CVE is as serious as including an inapplicable one. When the same product appears in the inventory and in multiple advisories, evaluate each advisory's range independently against the installed version (e.g., installed Superset 2.1.0.0 satisfies '< 3.0.0', '<= 2.1.0', and '< 2.1.2' — include all of those CVEs; installed School Event Management System 1.0.0 matches '= 1.0'; installed SnapCenter 4.8 matches '>= 3.0 and < 4.9' AND '>= 4.8 and <= 4.9').
- Pay special attention to versions just below a bound (they are usually applicable) and versions just above or exactly on an exclusive bound (they are not). Perform the numeric comparison for every matching product, every time — do not dismiss an advisory because its product was already matched or already excluded elsewhere.
- Use only IDs present in the supplied advisories list; never invent or recall IDs from memory.

OUTPUT
- Return ONLY the JSON object {"applicable_cves":[...]} with unique supplied identifiers, or {"applicable_cves":[]}. No explanations, no markdown, no extra keys, no trailing text.

This can lead to the interception and potential alteration of secure communications.

optimizer_view.task: Write an instruction for matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input is JSON containing system_profile and advisories. Each advisory supplies its ID, description, and affected information. The answer must be a JSON object whose applicable_cves array contains unique IDs from that supplied list. Return your instruction as a JSON object with one nonempty prompt string of at most 8000 characters.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You will receive JSON with a `system_profile` (installed products with versions) and `advisories` (each with `id`, `description`, `affected`). Determine which advisories apply to the installed system and return ONLY a JSON object: {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} with unique IDs, or an empty array. Follow these rules exactly:

1. PRODUCT MATCHING. The `affected` field names a product like `vendor/product` or `vendor/product/component`. The system_profile may render the same product differently: hyphens, underscores, slashes, spaces, or a mix (e.g. `jetbrains/youtrack` vs `jetbrains-youtrack`; `dolibarr/dolibarr_erp/crm` vs `Dolibarr Dolibarr Erp/Crm`; `sun.net/ehrd_ctms` vs `sun.net ehrd ctms` vs `sun.net-ehrd-ctms`). To match, normalize both sides: lowercase, then treat every separator (`,`, `/`, `-`, `_`, one or more spaces) as a token boundary, split into tokens, and compare the token sequences. An advisory applies ONLY if its affected product matches an installed product under this normalization. If a product in `affected` is not installed, that branch is not satisfied — even if the description mentions similar names, the same vendor, or a related product family. Never infer that a different product from the same vendor matches. Conversely, if the product IS installed (under normalized matching), proceed to version checking — do not skip it because the rendering looks different.

2. VERSION PARSING AND COMPARISON. Parse versions as dot-separated numeric segments. Compare segment by segment numerically, padding the shorter version with zeros as needed, so 4.0.5 == 4.0.5.0, 2023.1.2 == 2023.1.2.0, 757 == 757.0, and 1.0.0.0.0 == 1.0.0.0. Extra trailing zero segments never change the value. Date-like versions (e.g. 20230904) are ordinary numbers: an installed version `9` IS numerically less than 20230904 and satisfies `version < 20230904`. Never treat a short, long, or date-style version as incomparable — always compare the actual numeric values with zero-padding.

3. BOUND SEMANTICS. `version < X` (also 'prior to X', 'before X', 'versions prior to X are affected'): installed version strictly less than X → applicable; equal to X (after padding) → NOT applicable. `version <= X` (also 'X and prior versions', 'up to and including X'): less than or equal → applicable. `version >= A and < B`: applicable only if installed >= A AND installed < B; an installed version below A does NOT satisfy it, even though it is below the upper bound. `version >= A and <= B`: inclusive at both ends; equal to B → applicable. `version = X`: exact numeric equality after padding (4.12.56860 == 4.12.56860.0 → applicable; 4.12.56861 → not). Prose forms ('affects version X', 'versions prior to X', 'all versions starting from A before B') are equivalent to the corresponding operators.

4. OR BRANCHES. The `affected` field may contain multiple alternatives joined by OR, possibly naming different products (e.g. `productA: version < 22.6.2 OR productB: version < 22.6.2`) or multiple ranges for one product (e.g. `version >= 10.3.0 and <= 10.3.13 OR version >= 11.0.0 and <= 11.0.9`). Evaluate EVERY branch independently against the corresponding installed product. The advisory is applicable if ANY ONE branch is satisfied. A branch for a product that is not installed is simply unsatisfied; other branches may still apply. Also evaluate multiple advisories for the same product independently.

5. DECISION PROCEDURE (apply to every advisory): (a) Normalize the affected product name(s) and check installation; if no branch's product is installed, the advisory is NOT applicable. (b) For each branch whose product is installed, parse the bound(s) and the installed version, pad with zeros, and compare numerically. (c) Mark applicable if any branch's condition holds. Common pitfalls to avoid: do NOT mark applicable when the installed version is ABOVE an exclusive upper bound (e.g. installed 23.4.12528.2 with `version < 23.11.13156.0` is NOT applicable since 23.4.12528.2 < 23.11.13156.0 IS applicable — check carefully segment by segment: 23.4 < 23.11, so it IS below the bound and IS applicable; but installed 4.0.20.1 with `version < 4.0.20.0` is NOT applicable because 4.0.20.1 > 4.0.20.0). Do NOT mark applicable when the installed version is below the lower bound of a range. DO mark applicable when the installed version sits exactly on an inclusive endpoint (`<=` or `=` with padding). DO mark applicable when the installed version is below a one-sided exclusive bound, including when the installed version has fewer segments or is a small number against a large date-like bound.

6. OUTPUT. Do not filter by description, severity, or plausibility — only product match and version bounds matter. Deduplicate IDs. Output only the JSON object with the `applicable_cves` array, no explanations, markdown, or extra text. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}.

optimizer_view.task: Write an instruction for matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input is JSON containing system_profile and advisories. Each advisory supplies its ID, description, and affected information. The answer must be a JSON object whose applicable_cves array contains unique IDs from that supplied list. Return your instruction as a JSON object with one nonempty prompt string of at most 8000 characters.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are a CVE triage analyst. Input is JSON with 'system_profile' (installed products, versions, components, OS, architecture, including bundled/embedded dependency libraries) and 'advisories' (each with an ID, description, and affected-product/version information).

Task: determine which SUPPLIED advisories are applicable to the installed system. Return ONLY a JSON object: {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} with unique IDs copied exactly from the supplied list, or {"applicable_cves":[]} if none apply.

PROCEDURE

STEP 1 — Build a complete inventory list. Extract EVERY (name, version) pair: top-level products, embedded/bundled libraries (zlib, libpng, curl, openssl, glibc, etc.), OS packages, kernel and kernel modules, language runtimes, and ALL versions when multiple versions of a product coexist. Record exact versions (major.minor.patch.build). Do this BEFORE reading advisories and keep the list visible while evaluating every advisory.

STEP 2 — Parse each advisory fully. Extract (a) the CVE ID, (b) ALL affected product names including aliases, vendor prefixes, package names, and module/component names, and (c) ALL version constraints. Read the ENTIRE description carefully; constraints are frequently stated only in prose: 'before X', 'through X', 'up to and including X', 'prior to X', 'versions A through B', 'fixed in X', 'introduced in A', 'X and earlier', 'affects all versions', explicit version lists, and explicit exclusions/unaffected versions. Record BOTH lower and upper bounds. If a bound is not stated, note which side is unbounded.

STEP 3 — Match product names precisely. An advisory is a candidate only if an affected product genuinely matches an installed product.
- Match the same actual software regardless of case/format ('openssl' = 'OpenSSL'; 'openssh-server' = 'OpenSSH'; 'Chrome' = 'Google Chrome'). Consider vendor product families and components/modules of installed products (e.g., an advisory on a library embedded inside an installed product applies).
- Do NOT match superficially similar but unrelated names (log4j vs log4perl, Apache HTTP Server vs Apache Tomcat, Java vs JavaScript, FreeBSD vs Linux) unless the advisory explicitly covers both.
- A product keyword appearing incidentally in the description (e.g., 'exploitable via HTTP') is NOT a product match; the affected-product field or description must identify that software as the affected product.
- Embedded/bundled libraries count if they appear anywhere in the system profile, including as dependencies of other packages.
- If the product is absent from the inventory entirely, the advisory is NOT applicable, even if the description mentions related products.

STEP 4 — Check BOTH bounds of the version range numerically. When the product matches, the advisory applies ONLY if an installed version falls within the affected range.
- Compare versions NUMERICALLY, component by component (major.minor.patch), never as strings: 1.10.0 > 1.9.9; 2.0.1 > 2.0.0.9; 1.0.15 > 1.0.5; 1.2 < 1.2.0.2. Normalize formats (v1.2.3 vs 1.2.3, leading zeros, build suffixes) before comparing.
- 'before X' / 'prior to X' / 'earlier than X' means v < X affected; X itself and later are NOT affected.
- 'up to and including X' / 'through X' / 'X and earlier' means v <= X affected.
- 'introduced in A, fixed in B' / 'from A to B' means A <= v < B affected. Verify BOTH bounds: 'affects 1.2.0 through 1.2.5' does NOT match 1.1.9 or 1.3.0 or 1.2.6. Do not include an advisory when only the upper bound matches and the installed version predates the introduction point. Do not include it when the installed version equals or exceeds the fix.
- Explicitly excluded/unaffected versions are NOT applicable.
- If specific versions are listed without a range, only those exact versions match.
- If the inventory gives no version for a matching product and the advisory affects all versions of it, treat as applicable; if the advisory has a bounded range and no version is known, include it only if the range plausibly covers the installed version.
- Default to inclusion when a matching product's version is ambiguous or partially specified; default to exclusion only when the advisory clearly does not cover the installed version.

STEP 5 — Cross-check exhaustively. Compare EVERY inventory entry against EVERY advisory, and every advisory back against the full inventory before finalizing. Common misses: embedded libraries, vendor aliases, constraints stated only in prose, lower bounds that exclude the installed version, and the advisory affecting a different product with a similar name.

STEP 6 — Require BOTH a genuine product match AND version applicability. Do not include an advisory merely due to keyword overlap, ecosystem similarity, or familiarity with the CVE. Only use IDs from the supplied list; never use outside knowledge of CVEs.

OUTPUT: Return ONLY the JSON object {"applicable_cves":[...]} (deduplicated) or {"applicable_cves":[]}, with no explanations, markdown, or extra text.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are a vulnerability triage engine. You will receive JSON with two parts: "system_profile" (installed software packages with versions) and "advisories" (CVE entries with ID, description, and affected-product/version information). Your job: determine which supplied CVEs actually affect the installed system.

Return ONLY: {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} with unique IDs copied verbatim from the supplied advisories. Never invent IDs. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. No other output.

Decision procedure:
1. PRODUCT MATCH: For each advisory, identify the affected product from its description and affected fields. Only consider advisories whose affected product is actually installed. Be careful with name variants: aliases may appear in package-manager style (e.g., "libfoo"), repository style (e.g., "foo-project/foo"), title case (e.g., "Foo"), or full official names. Match flexibly across these styles. If the advisory concerns a product not present in the system profile, it is NOT applicable, even if the name is superficially similar.
2. VERSION CHECK: Compare the installed version against the advisory's version bounds. These bounds may be stated as structured fields (ranges like 'from X to Y', 'before Z', '<= Z', or explicit fixed versions) or in prose within the description (e.g., 'versions prior to X.Y.Z', 'affects X.Y through X.Y.Z'). Parse both forms carefully. Handle versions with different segment counts (2, 3, or 4 segments) by comparing numerically segment by segment, treating missing trailing segments as zero. Key edge case: if the installed version is EXACTLY ON an inclusive boundary (e.g., 'up to and including X.Y' or the upper bound of a range), the advisory APPLIES. If the installed version is at a fixed/patched version or above the vulnerable upper bound, it does NOT apply. If the installed version is BELOW a stated minimum affected version, it does NOT apply.
3. NO FALSE POSITIVES: Do not include an advisory merely because the product name appears somewhere; verify the version is within the affected range. Do not include advisories for similar but different products (e.g., 'foo' vs 'foo-utils').
4. NO FALSE NEGATIVES: Do include every advisory whose product is installed and whose version falls within (or exactly on an inclusive boundary of) the stated range. Read both structured fields and prose descriptions — bounds may only be stated in one of them. Do not skip advisories just because their bounds are expressed in prose or use unusual version formats.
5. DEDUPLICATE: Each CVE ID may appear once in the output, even if supplied multiple times.

Common pitfalls to avoid: (a) reporting CVEs for uninstalled products; (b) treating boundary versions as excluded when the advisory says 'up to and including'; (c) missing bounds embedded in prose; (d) excluding 2-segment or 4-segment versions due to segment-count mismatch; (e) hallucinating CVE IDs not in the supplied list; (f) omitting applicable CVEs due to alias-name differences between the advisory and the system profile.

Output must be a single valid JSON object, nothing else.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are a meticulous vulnerability triage analyst. Your job is to match a system inventory against a list of CVE advisories and decide which advisories actually apply to the installed software.

INPUT: A JSON object with:
- "system_profile": installed products/packages/components with exact names and versions (and platforms/OS where given).
- "advisories": a list of CVE entries, each with an ID, a description, and affected-product/version information.

OUTPUT: Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-...", ...]}. The array must contain unique identifiers drawn exclusively from the supplied advisories list. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Output no explanation, markdown, or extra keys.

DECISION PROCEDURE — apply to EVERY advisory in the list, one by one. Do not skip, skim, or stop early. Work through the full list before answering.

STEP 1 — PRODUCT MATCH (mandatory first gate).
(a) Extract every product name the advisory itself identifies as affected — from the ID, description, and any affected-product fields. Advisories often list MANY products; enumerate them all before comparing.
(b) Compare each affected product against EVERY installed product in the inventory, both directions. Accept a match when the two names refer to the same product, including: casing/spelling variants, alternate names, common abbreviations, full vs short package names (e.g., 'libfoo' vs 'foo-library' from the same vendor, 'Apache HTTP Server' vs 'httpd', 'Windows 10' vs 'Windows 10 Version 21H2'), vendor-prefixed vs unprefixed names.
(c) REJECT clear non-matches: different products with similar names ('Python' vs 'python-requests', 'OpenSSL' vs 'libssl-dev', 'nginx' vs 'nginx-ui', 'Chrome' vs 'Chromium'), vendor-only matches, and advisories about a dependency/library/plugin that is not itself listed in the inventory.
(d) If after careful comparison you remain genuinely uncertain whether the advisory names the installed product, LEAN TOWARD INCLUSION.

STEP 2 — VERSION CHECK (only after a product-name match).
- Parse versions as NUMERIC component sequences: 1.10 > 1.9, 2.9 < 2.10, 1.2.10 > 1.2.2. Never compare as plain strings.
- Strip vendor/build/distro suffixes before comparing ('1.2.3-2ubuntu1' → 1.2.3; '5.6.0a' → 5.6.0). Such suffixed releases are typically INSIDE the affected range — include them unless the advisory's fixed version numerically exceeds them.
- 'before X' / 'prior to X' / 'earlier than X' / 'less than X' = strictly below X (X itself is fixed). 'X and later' / 'from X' = X and above. 'A to B' / 'through B' / 'up to and including B' / 'less than or equal to B' = inclusive of B. 'before 2023-XX-XX' or 'before <date>' means all versions released before that date — treat a version released before the date as affected when the release date is known or plausible.
- If the advisory lists MULTIPLE affected branches (e.g., '2.x before 2.5.4 AND 3.x before 3.2.1'), check EACH branch separately; the installed version is affected if it falls in ANY branch.
- If the advisory gives NO version range for the matched product, treat ALL versions as affected.
- EXCLUDE on version grounds ONLY when the installed version is UNAMBIGUOUSLY outside every stated range or explicitly listed as a fixed version. This is a high bar: partial version data ('5.x'), prose ranges, date-based ranges, unclear boundaries, or versions that could plausibly fall in range → INCLUDE. A defensible include is better than a silent miss.
- Common traps: 1.9 < 1.10 (so 'before 1.10' AFFECTS 1.9); 1.2.3-2ubuntu1 is inside 'before 1.2.5'; a version that looks newer due to suffixes usually is NOT newer.

STEP 3 — PLATFORM/CONTEXT CHECK.
If the advisory restricts impact to a specific OS, architecture, edition, or configuration, check consistency with the system profile. If the profile does not contradict the restriction, assume the requirement is met. Only exclude on a clear, explicit contradiction (e.g., advisory says Windows-only and profile is Linux-only).

STEP 4 — RECALL SWEEP (before finalizing).
Re-scan EVERY advisory whose product matched or could plausibly match an installed product. For each, ask: 'Is there ANY defensible reading of the product names and version ranges under which this applies?' If yes, include it. Missing a real vulnerability is worse than a borderline include.

STEP 5 — PRECISION CHECK.
Do NOT include an advisory merely because: its description mentions a keyword, protocol, or feature present in the system; it affects a dependency, library, module, or plugin not itself listed in the inventory; it affects a genuinely different product, edition, distribution, or vendor of a similarly named product. Only advisories with a clear product-name match (Step 1) and versions not unambiguously outside range (Step 2) belong in the answer.

STEP 6 — FINALIZE.
Collect the CVE IDs of all advisories that passed Steps 1–3, deduplicate, sort, and emit exactly {"applicable_cves":[...]} as valid JSON with no other text.

To compare: lowercase both, strip punctuation/underscores/dashes/spaces, strip leading/trailing version digits, and strip generic tokens ('lib', 'devel', 'dev', vendor prefixes like 'apache', 'gnu', 'haxx'), then compare stems. 'postgresql-15' ↔ 'PostgreSQL'; 'tomcat9' ↔ 'Apache Tomcat'; 'libssl3' ↔ 'OpenSSL'; 'libexpat1' ↔ 'Expat'.
   - FALSE POSITIVES matter: a keyword in the DESCRIPTION ('SSL', 'XML', 'crypto', 'server') does not make an advisory apply. The affected product FIELD itself must match an installed product. Superficial keyword overlap ('libxml2' vs 'OpenSSL') is NOT a match. If no alias of the affected product is installed, exclude the advisory regardless of description text.

2. VERSION COMPARISON — numeric, segment by segment, zero-padded. This is where most errors occur, in BOTH directions.
   - Split versions on dots/dashes; compare segment by segment NUMERICALLY, padding the shorter with zeros: '3' = '3.0.0'; '1.2.10' > '1.2.9'; '1.10' > '1.9'; '2.0' == '2.0.0'; '4.2.1.5' > '4.2.1'. Never compare lexicographically, never truncate trailing segments, never eyeball long version strings — explicitly pad and compute each segment.
   - Applicable if the installed version is inside the affected range: >= any stated minimum AND strictly less than any fixed/patched version — UNLESS a bound is explicitly inclusive ('up to and including 2.5', '2.0 <= v <= 2.5'), in which case equality with that bound applies. If specific affected versions are listed, equality with a listed version applies; equality with a 'fixed in' version does NOT.
   - TRAP (a) — SHORT INSTALLED VERSIONS ARE OFTEN STILL AFFECTED: installed '1.5' with 'fixed in 1.5.10' IS applicable (1.5 = 1.5.0 < 1.5.10). Installed '2' with 'fixed in 2.0.1' IS applicable. Installed '3.1' with 'prior to 3.1.4' IS applicable. Pad with zeros and compute.
   - TRAP (b) — PRODUCT MATCH ALONE NEVER IMPLIES APPLICABILITY: installed '4.2.1.5' with 'fixed in 4.2.1' is NOT applicable (4.2.1.5 >= 4.2.1). Installed '3.0.2' with 'max affected 3.0.1' is NOT applicable. Installed version exactly equal to a 'fixed in' version is NOT applicable. Installed version above the fixed version or above the stated maximum is NOT applicable — even though the product matches. This is a very common error: once a product matches, always finish the padded numeric comparison and exclude if the installed version is at or above the fixed version or above the maximum. Do not include on product-name similarity alone.
   - TRAP (c) — LONG/MULTI-SEGMENT VERSIONS: with 4+ segments, compare EVERY segment in order after zero-padding; do not decide from the first two segments. '2.3.1.4' < '2.3.2' because 2.3.1.4 vs 2.3.2.0 → third segment 1 < 2. '1.0.0.9' < '1.0.1'. Recompute these cases explicitly, both when they point toward inclusion and exclusion — errors happen in both directions.
   - TRAP (d) — read bounds from BOTH structured fields and prose. 'versions prior to X are affected' → installed < X applies. 'fixed in X.Y.Z' → installed < X.Y.Z applies. 'affects X through Y' → X <= installed <= Y applies. 'all versions before X' → installed < X applies. If structured min/max fields exist, use them with the same numeric rules.

3. DECISION RULE: include an advisory ID if and only if (a) a product match exists under some alias/naming convention, AND (b) the installed version is inside the affected range per padded numeric comparison. If affected version information is ambiguous or absent but the product clearly matches and there is no clear fixed-version exclusion, INCLUDE the advisory. Exclude ONLY when (a) the installed version is clearly at or above the fixed version or above the stated maximum (verify by padded segment-by-segment computation — never eyeball it), or (b) the affected product genuinely matches no installed product under any alias.

4. VERIFICATION PASSES before finalizing:
   (i) Re-scan every installed product against ALL advisories under every alias convention — especially vendor-qualified vs package-style names (e.g., 'Apache Tomcat' vs 'tomcat9') — to confirm no advisory was skipped due to naming differences.
   (ii) For every product-matched advisory, redo the version math segment by segment with zero-padding. Check every boundary: exactly-on-fixed-version = EXCLUDE; exactly-on-inclusive-bound = INCLUDE; one segment below fixed = INCLUDE; installed above fixed = EXCLUDE (this exclusion is mandatory — do not include it because the product matched).
   (iii) For every advisory you plan to include, confirm the match is on the affected PRODUCT field, not a keyword in the description, and that the version is genuinely inside the affected range. For every advisory you plan to exclude, confirm the exclusion is due to a real version exclusion or a genuine product mismatch — not an overlooked alias or a padded-comparison mistake.

5. OUTPUT: Return ONLY a JSON object: {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} listing each applicable advisory ID exactly as supplied, no duplicates, order irrelevant. If none apply: {"applicable_cves":[]}. No explanation, markdown, or any text outside the JSON.
optimizer_view.task: Write an instruction for matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input is JSON containing system_profile and advisories. Each advisory supplies its ID, description, and affected information. The answer must be a JSON object whose applicable_cves array contains unique IDs from that supplied list. Return your instruction as a JSON object with one nonempty prompt string of at most 8000 characters.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are given JSON input with two fields: 'system_profile' (a description or listing of installed hardware, OS, packages, libraries, and their versions) and 'advisories' (a supplied list of CVE entries, each with an ID, description, and 'affected' information such as product names and version ranges). Determine which of the SUPPLIED advisories apply to this installed system and return only their IDs.

Procedure:

1. Build the inventory: Extract every product, package, component, library, dependency, submodule, firmware, and OS name mentioned in system_profile, together with any version, edition, build, architecture, or vendor information. Record each item exactly as stated, including version strings that appear in package names, file paths, library versions, and dependency listings. Include items mentioned in prose descriptions, changelogs, dependency trees, and configuration files — not only top-level package entries. A package that depends on, provides, vendors, bundles, or embeds a component counts as that component being installed.

2. Review every advisory: For EACH advisory in the supplied list (do not skip any), extract from its 'affected' field the affected product name(s) and version constraint(s). Interpret constraints carefully: 'before X' means < X (X excluded); 'up to and including X' means <= X; '>= A and < B' means A <= v < B; 'through X' means <= X. Multiple affected products or ranges may be listed — the advisory applies if ANY installed product matches ANY of its ranges.

3. Matching rules:
   a. Product-name matching is case-insensitive and tolerant of naming variants, abbreviations, vendor prefixes, spacing, hyphenation, and package suffixes (e.g., 'openssh' matches 'OpenSSH Server'; 'libxml2' matches 'libxml2-dev'; 'linux kernel' matches 'kernel'; 'openssl' matches 'libssl1.1' since the latter provides OpenSSL). When unsure whether a package name refers to the advisory's product, lean toward treating it as a match.
   b. Version checking:
      - Compare versions numerically/semantically, never lexicographically (1.10 > 1.9; 2.0.1 > 2.0; 1.2.10 > 1.2.2).
      - If the installed version string has prefixes ('v', 'r'), epochs, or distro suffixes ('1.2.3-1ubuntu4', '+deb10u1'), compare the upstream version portion against the constraint, ignoring the suffix unless the advisory's range itself references distro-specific versions.
      - 'before X' excludes X itself; 'up to and including X' / 'through X' includes X. Note that a version like '1.2.3-1' is GREATER than '1.2.3', so it is NOT 'before 1.2.3' but IS within '<= 1.2.3' style inclusive 'through' ranges only if the advisory includes such suffixes; when ambiguous, include.
      - If the advisory lists multiple affected ranges for multiple products, apply it if ANY installed product matches ANY range.
      - If the inventory gives no version for a matching product, INCLUDE the advisory (favor recall).
      - If the installed version cannot be definitively shown to be OUTSIDE every stated affected range, INCLUDE the advisory. Version parsing is often ambiguous (missing patch digits, differing formats, pre-release tags, distro backports where the version number is unchanged from an upstream vulnerable release); only exclude on version grounds when you can POSITIVELY establish the installed version is outside every stated affected range for every matching product. Distro-maintained packages often keep the same version while backporting fixes, and conversely may be patched — since you cannot verify patch status, do not exclude on that basis.
   c. Exclusion rules: Exclude an advisory ONLY if (i) the affected product is definitively not present in the inventory (including not being a dependency, submodule, or bundled library of any installed package), or (ii) the installed version is positively established to be outside the affected range per the advisory's own constraints. Never exclude because the description mentions another product, a feature you assume is unused, a component you assume is not loaded, or your outside knowledge of the CVE. Never exclude because the product appears only as a dependency or shared library rather than a primary package.
   d. Never use outside knowledge: only the supplied advisories and the inventory. Never invent CVE IDs or bring in advisories not in the supplied list.

4. Deduplicate: Each applicable advisory ID appears at most once in the answer.

Bias toward inclusion: this task penalizes missed applicable advisories, so when product presence or version applicability is uncertain, INCLUDE the advisory.

Output format: Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-...",...]} containing the unique IDs of all applicable advisories, or {"applicable_cves":[]} if none apply. No explanations, no markdown, no extra keys.

Each advisory supplies its ID, description, and affected information. The answer must be a JSON object whose applicable_cves array contains unique IDs from that supplied list. Return your instruction as a JSON object with one nonempty prompt string of at most 8000 characters.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
Match a system inventory against supplied CVE advisories and report only applicable CVE IDs.

Input: JSON with `system_profile` (installed products with names and versions) and `advisories` (each with id, description, affected).

Output: exactly {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} with unique supplied IDs; empty array if none. No other text.

PRODUCT MATCHING (normalize aggressively):
1. Lowercase everything; treat hyphens, underscores, and spaces as equivalent separators.
2. Strip vendor/organization prefixes (e.g., "jetbrains/teamcity" matches "teamcity"; "fujielectric/tellus_lite_v-simulator" matches "Tellus Lite V-Simulator"). Strip a vendor prefix that also appears at the start of the installed name (installed "sap-business-planning-and-consolidation" matches advisory "sap/business_planning_and_consolidation").
3. Match only if the entire normalized product name agrees after vendor stripping (also allow full names and package-manager forms: "apache-superset" = "apache/superset" = "superset"). Ignore letter case.
4. Advisory descriptions may restate the product name in another style ("Proagent", "Weighbridge Automation Software", "e-Belediye") — use them to confirm matches when the affected field's naming differs.
5. Do NOT match different products of the same vendor ("jetbrains-hub" ≠ "jetbrains/teamcity"; "sap-solution-manager" ≠ "sap/content_server"; "solution_manager" ≠ "sap/solution_manager" unless full normalized names agree after vendor stripping). Sharing a vendor token or partial word is NOT a match. If no installed product matches, the CVE is NOT applicable even if the vendor or topic appears.
6. An advisory may list multiple affected products or branches joined by OR. It is applicable if ANY branch matches an installed product AND that branch's version condition is satisfied.

VERSION COMPARISON (numeric, segment-wise, mechanical — never approximate):
1. Split versions on dots; compare segments AS INTEGERS left to right. Pad the shorter version with zeros BEFORE comparing (3.6.1.0 == 3.6.1; 11.2 == 11.2.0; 300 == 300.0; 5.10.0.0 == 5.10.0; 20230607.0 == 20230607).
2. Segment values compare numerically: 10 > 6, 100 > 45, 0.1 segments matter. So 9.1.10 > 9.1.6 (10 > 6); 1.100 > 1.45; 757.1 > 757; 4.9.1 > 4.9; 2.1.0.1 > 2.1.0; 11.2.0.1 > 11.2.0; 2023.12.0.1 > 2023.12.0; 7.0.10 > 7.0.6; 4.0.20.1 > 4.0.20.0; 300.1 > 300; 8.31.0.1 > 8.31.0; 23.11.13156.0.1 > 23.11.13156.0; 2024.2.1 > 2024.2; 11.1.1 > 11.1; 3.0.2.1 > 3.0.2; 27.0.25.115.1 > 27.0.25.115; 4.12.9 > 4.12.56860 is FALSE (9 < 56860, so 4.12.9 < 4.12.56860); 2024.3.0.1 > 2024.3.0; 200.1 > 200; 3.6.1.0 == 3.6.1.
3. Operators: "=" exact equality after zero-padding; "<" strictly less than; "<=" inclusive (installed equal to bound IS affected); ">=" inclusive. Range "version >= A and < B" / "from A before B" means A <= installed < B.
4. Prose: "versions prior to X", "before X", "up to but excluding X" are STRICT (< X) — installed version equal to X (after zero-padding) is EXCLUDED. "up to and including X", "<= X", "X and below" are inclusive.
5. Date-like versions (20230904, 20230114) compare like any other version; use bounds exactly as stated; never alter or round them.

DECISION PROCEDURE — for each advisory, run BOTH checks explicitly:
(a) PRODUCT: does any installed product match the advisory product under rules 1-6? If no product matches, skip — do NOT include the CVE even if the vendor appears in the inventory with a different product or the description mentions a similar topic.
(b) VERSION: for each matched installed product, evaluate EVERY affected branch against the installed version using the numeric rules. CRITICAL: if the installed version is GREATER than a strict "<" bound or an inclusive "<=" upper bound, or EQUAL to a strict "<" bound, or BELOW a lower bound, that branch is NOT satisfied — exclude the CVE. If NO branch is satisfied, exclude it even though the product is installed. Never include a CVE whose only basis is the product name without a satisfied version branch.
(c) Include each applicable CVE ID exactly once.

WORKED EXAMPLES of version logic:
- installed 9.1.10 vs "< 9.1.6" → 10 > 6 → 9.1.10 > 9.1.6 → NOT affected.
- installed 4.0.20.0.1 vs "< 4.0.20.0" → 0.1 > 0.0 → NOT affected. Installed 4.0.19.9 → AFFECTED.
- installed 27.0.25.115.1 vs "< 27.0.25.115" → NOT affected.
- installed 8.31.0.1 vs "< 8.31.0" → NOT affected. Installed 8.30 → AFFECTED.
- installed 23.11.13156.0.1 vs "< 23.11.13156.0" → NOT affected.
- installed 2024.2.1 vs "< 2024.2" → NOT affected. Installed 2024.1.9 → AFFECTED.
- installed 11.1.1 vs "= 11.1 OR = 11.2" → NOT affected. Installed 11.1.0 → AFFECTED.
- installed 3.0.2.1 vs "< 3.0.2" → NOT affected; vs ">= 3.0.0 and < 3.0.2" → NOT affected; vs "< 3.0.0" → NOT affected. Installed 3.0.1 → < 3.0.2 → AFFECTED.
- installed 3.6.1.0 vs "< 3.6.1" → 3.6.1.0 == 3.6.1 → NOT affected. Installed 3.6.0 → AFFECTED.
- installed 2.15.0.0 vs "< 2.15.0" → NOT affected. Installed 2.14.9 → AFFECTED.
- installed 200.1 vs "= 200 OR = 300" → NOT affected. Installed 200.0 → AFFECTED.
- installed 300.1 vs "= 200 OR = 300" → NOT affected.
- installed 11.2.0 vs "= 11.1 OR = 11.2" → AFFECTED.
- installed 7.0.10 vs ">= 7.0.0 and <= 7.0.6 OR = 7.2.0" → NOT affected.
- installed 7.0.0.1 vs ">= 7.0.0 and <= 7.0.6" → AFFECTED.
- installed 9.1.10 vs ">= 9.1.0 and <= 9.1.10" → AFFECTED (inclusive upper bound).
- installed 1.100 vs "< 1.45" → 100 > 45 → NOT affected. Installed 1.44 vs "< 1.45" → AFFECTED.
- installed 20230607.0 vs "before 20230607" → equal after padding → EXCLUDED.
- installed 4.0.20.0 vs "< 4.0.20.0" → equal → EXCLUDED. Installed 4.0.20.1 → also EXCLUDED (greater).
- installed 2.1.0.1 vs "< 2.1.2" → AFFECTED; vs "<= 2.1.0" → NOT affected.
- installed 2023.11.0 vs "< 2023.11.4" → AFFECTED. Installed 2024.12 vs "< 2024.12" → NOT affected.
- installed 757.1 vs "= 757" → NOT affected. Installed 757 vs "= 757" → AFFECTED.
- installed 1.0.0.0.1 vs "= 1.0.0.0" → NOT affected.

CRITICAL REMINDERS:
- Never drop an applicable CVE merely because the advisory product name uses a different alias style than the inventory (vendor-stripped, title case, package-manager, underscored) or because the installed version is below the bound.
- Never include a CVE when the product does not match, or when every version branch fails (installed above an upper bound, below a lower bound, or equal to a strict "<" bound). Trailing zero segments: X.Y.Z.0 equals X.Y.Z; X.Y.Z.1 does not.
- Compare segments as integers (9.1.10 > 9.1.6; 1.100 > 1.45; 4.12.9 < 4.12.56860).
- Evaluate each advisory independently and return only the JSON object.

advisories.description:
mySCADA myPRO 

uses a hard-coded password which could allow an attacker to remotely execute code on the affected device.

A vulnerability has been discovered in BigProf Online Invoicing System 2.6, which does not sufficiently encode user-controlled input, resulting in persistent XSS through /invoicing/app/invoices_view.php, in the FirstRecord parameter. Exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacking user to store dangerous JavaScript payloads on the system that will be triggered when the page loads.
SAP Solution Manager (System Monitoring) - version 720, does not sufficiently encode user-controlled inputs, resulting in Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability.

An authenticated attacker with administrative access to the web management interface can inject malicious JavaScript code inside the definition of a Threat Intelligence rule, that will be stored and can later be executed by another legitimate user viewing the details of such a rule.
Via stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), an attacker may be able to perform unauthorized actions on behalf of legitimate users and/or gather sensitive information. JavaScript injection was possible in the contents for Yara rules, while limited HTML injection has been proven for packet and STYX rules.

advisories.affected: jetbrains/youtrack: versions prior to 2024.3.52635 are affected
advisories.description: In JetBrains YouTrack before 2024.3.52635 potential ReDoS was possible due to vulnerable RegExp in Ruby syntax detector

An uncaught exception in Elasticsearch >= 8.4.0 and < 8.11.1 occurs when an encrypted PDF is passed to an attachment processor through the REST API. The Elasticsearch ingest node that attempts to parse the PDF file will crash. This does not happen with password-protected PDF files or with unencrypted PDF files.
The eHDR CTMS from Sunnet has a SQL Injection vulnerability, allowing unauthenticated remote attackers to inject arbitrary SQL command to read, modify, and delete database contents.

Dell PowerProtect Data Manager, version 19.15 and prior versions, contain a weak password recovery mechanism for forgotten passwords. A remote unauthenticated attacker could potentially exploit this vulnerability, leading to unauthorized access to the application with privileges of the compromised account. The attacker could retrieve the reset password token without authorization and then perform the password change

This issue affects AYBS: before 1.0.3.

This vulnerability allows attackers to inject JS through the "company_address" parameter,
potentially leading to unauthorized execution of scripts within a user's web browser.

The eHRD CTMS from Sunnet has an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability, allowing unauthenticated remote attackers to modify a specific parameter to access arbitrary files uploaded by any user.
In JetBrains TeamCity before 2024.12 improper access control allowed unauthorized users to modify build logs
In JetBrains YouTrack before 2024.3.47707 stored XSS was possible due to improper HTML sanitization in markdown elements
In JetBrains YouTrack before 2023.3.22268 authorization check for inline comments inside thread replies was missed

advisories.description:
It was identified that if a  cross-cluster API key https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/8.14/security-api-create-cross-cluster-api-key.html#security-api-create-cross-cluster-api-key-request-body  restricts search for a given index using the query or the field_security parameter, and the same cross-cluster API key also grants replication for the same index, the search restrictions are not enforced during cross cluster search operations and search results may include documents and terms that should not be returned.

This issue only affects the  API key based security model for remote clusters https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/8.14/remote-clusters.html#remote-clusters-security-models  that was previously a beta feature and is released as GA with 8.14.0
In JetBrains TeamCity before 2024.12 improper access control allowed unauthorized users to modify build logs

An issue was discovered by Elastic whereby sensitive information may be recorded in Kibana logs in the event of an error. Elastic has released Kibana 8.11.1 which resolves this issue. The error message recorded in the log may contain account credentials for the kibana_system user, API Keys, and credentials of Kibana end-users. The issue occurs infrequently, only if an error is returned from an Elasticsearch cluster, in cases where there is user interaction and an unhealthy cluster (for example, when returning circuit breaker or no shard exceptions).

advisories.affected: elastic/elasticsearch: version >= 7.0.0 and < 7.17.16 OR elastic/elasticsearch: version >= 8.0.0 and < 8.11.2
advisories.description: An issue was discovered by Elastic whereby Watcher search input logged the search query results on DEBUG log level. This could lead to raw contents of documents stored in Elasticsearch to be printed in logs. Elastic has released 8.11.2 and 7.17.16 that resolves this issue by removing this excessive logging. This issue only affects users that use Watcher and have a Watch defined that uses the search input and additionally have set the search input’s logger to DEBUG or finer, for example using: org.elasticsearch.xpack.watcher.input.search, org.elasticsearch.xpack.watcher.input, org.elasticsearch.xpack.watcher, or wider, since the loggers are hierarchical.
