optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are given a JSON input with a system_profile (installed products and versions) and an advisories list (each with an id, description, and affected field). Determine which supplied CVEs apply to the installed system and return ONLY {"applicable_cves":[...]} with unique IDs copied verbatim from the input. Follow these rules carefully.

1. PRODUCT MATCHING — ALIASES ARE THE SAME PRODUCT. The advisory 'affected' field uses 'vendor/product' identifiers. Inventory names may look different but refer to the SAME product: package-manager style ('jetbrains-youtrack'), repo style with underscores ('sap/solution_manager', 'hyperview/geoportal_toolkit'), or display names with spaces and capitals ('Sportsnet Sportsnet', 'jetbrains webstorm'). To compare, normalize BOTH sides: lowercase, then convert '/', '_', spaces, and all punctuation to '-', then collapse repeated dashes. Compare the full normalized string AND also the product component alone (the part after the vendor '/' in the advisory; the last components of the inventory name). Underscores in advisories are equivalent to dashes in inventory: 'solution_manager' = 'sap-solution-manager' = 'solution-manager'; 'geoportal_toolkit' = 'hyperview-geoportal-toolkit' = 'geoportal-toolkit'; 'weighbridge_automation_software' = 'uzaybaskul-weighbridge-automation-software'. 'libsoup' = 'gnome/libsoup'; 'total_security' = 'bitdefender-total-security'; 'job_portal' = 'phpgurukul-job-portal'; 'ehrd_ctms' = 'sun.net ehrd ctms' = 'ehrd-ctms'. If the product component matches after normalization, the product IS installed — do not skip it because the style differs. Do NOT match similarly-named unrelated products: 'sap-content-server' is NOT 'sap/solution_manager' or 'sap/abap_platform'; 'fortinac' is NOT 'fortiportal' or 'fortiwlm'; 'hub' is NOT 'teamcity' or 'youtrack'. Same vendor + different product component = no match.

2. VERSION COMPARISON — ALWAYS NUMERIC. Parse versions as tuples of integers split on '.', compare segment by segment numerically, never as strings. PREFIX RULE: compare the common prefix first; extra trailing segments in the inventory decide nothing once the common prefix is decided. inventory 4.12.56860.1 vs advisory = 4.12.56860 → first three segments equal → EQUAL. Trailing zeros never matter: 720.0 = 720; 7.15.0 = 7.15; 2.1.0.0 = 2.1.0; 1.0.0 = 1.0; 20230904.0 = 20230904; 4.10.0.0 vs bound 4.10.0 → equal; 9.0.18.0 = 9.0.18; 19.2 < 19.15 is FALSE (19.2 > 19.15 numerically: 2 < 15 segment-wise); 4.10 > 4.9 numerically.

3. BOUNDARIES — EXACT SEMANTICS.
- '< X' / 'before X' / 'prior to X' / 'versions prior to X are affected': applicable only if installed < X STRICTLY. If installed equals X after trailing-zero/prefix normalization (e.g. installed 1.1.1? no — installed 1.1 vs < 1.1 → NOT applicable; installed 1.0.2 vs < 1.0.3 → applicable), it is NOT applicable.
- '<= X' / 'up to and including X' / 'X and prior': applicable if installed <= X, EQUALITY INCLUDED. Installed 19.2 with '<= 19.15' → 19.2 > 19.15 → NOT applicable. Installed 2.1.0.0 with '<= 2.1.0' → applicable. Installed 9.2.8.1 with '<= 9.2.8' → prefix equal → applicable. Installed 8.5.4.0 with '<= 8.5.4' → applicable.
- '= X': applicable if installed equals X per prefix/trailing-zero rules. Multi-value equality ('= 11.1 OR = 11.2', '= 7.53'): applicable if installed equals ANY listed value. Installed 7.53.1 vs '= 7.53' → prefix (7,53) equal → EQUAL → applicable. Installed 4.12.56860 vs '= 4.12.56860' → applicable.
- Ranges '>= A and <= B': both inclusive. '>= A and < B': A inclusive, B exclusive. 'from A before B' = '>= A and < B'. Installed 3.7.1 with '>= 3.0.0 and < 3.7.2' → applicable. Installed 8.11.1.1 with '>= 8.10.0 and < 8.14.0' → applicable; with '>= 8.4.0 and < 8.11.1' → 8.11.1.1 vs 8.11.1 prefix equal → equal, NOT < bound → NOT applicable.
- LOWER BOUNDS MATTER: '>= A and < B' is NOT satisfied when installed < A, even though installed < B. Installed 7.0.1 with '>= 7.0.0 and < 7.17.16' → 7.0.1 >= 7.0.0 → applicable. Installed 7.0.1 with '>= 8.0.0 and < 8.11.2' → below lower bound → NOT applicable.
- OR of multiple conditions/ranges (e.g. 'fortiwlm: >= 8.5.0 and <= 8.5.4 OR fortiwlm: >= 8.6.0 and <= 8.6.5'; 'nozominetworks/cmc: < 22.6.3 OR guardian: >= 23.0.0 and < 23.1.0'): the advisory applies if ANY single condition is satisfied for a matching installed product. Installed guardian 22.6.2.0 with 'guardian < 22.6.3' → applicable. Installed 22.6.3.1 with '< 22.6.3' → not <, but check every other OR branch before rejecting.

4. WHERE TO READ BOUNDS. The structured 'affected' field is authoritative. Descriptions often restate bounds in prose ('before 3.0.0', 'from 1.0.0.95 before 1.0.0.100', 'versions 5.5.3 and prior', 'up to and including 2.1.0', 'version 19.15 and prior versions', 'up to but excluding X'). Use both; when they conflict, the structured field wins.

5. COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID.
- MISSING APPLICABLE CVEs IS THE MOST COSTLY ERROR. Re-check EVERY advisory whose product matches the inventory after normalization, especially when: the installed version is strictly below the fixed version (typical applicable case: YouTrack 2023.3.22269 < 2024.3.47707 → applicable; aybs 1.0.2 < 1.0.3 → applicable; snapcenter 4.10 with '>= 3.0 and < 4.9' → 4.10 > 4.9 → NOT applicable); the installed version sits exactly ON an inclusive bound ('=' or '<=' with trailing zeros, prefix-equal versions); the inventory name uses a different alias style (dashes vs slashes vs underscores vs spaces) than the advisory. If the product is installed and ANY condition is satisfied, INCLUDE the CVE.
- Do NOT include a CVE whose product is not actually installed, even if its description mentions that product or other products in prose (e.g. advisories for Bitdefender, osCommerce, FortiPortal, TeamCity, Apache Superset when only YouTrack/Kibana/etc. are installed). Prose mentions do not count — only inventory entries do.
- Do NOT include a CVE when the installed version is outside the range: installed equals an exclusive upper bound ('< X' with installed == X after normalization) → NOT applicable; installed above the bound → NOT applicable; installed below a range's lower bound ('>= A') → NOT applicable even if it is also < the upper bound.
- Do not compare version strings lexicographically: 19.2 vs 19.15 → 19.2 is GREATER (2 < 15 as integers); 4.10 vs 4.9 → 4.10 is GREATER; 20230914 vs 20230913 → greater.

6. PROCEDURE. For each advisory: (a) split 'affected' on ' OR ' and extract each product + version condition; (b) normalize names (slashes, underscores, dashes, spaces, punctuation → '-') and find a matching installed product by full name OR product component; (c) if found, compare the installed version numerically against EACH condition, honoring prefix-equality and trailing-zero rules; (d) if ANY condition is satisfied, include the advisory's id verbatim. After processing all advisories, deduplicate IDs. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Output ONLY the JSON object, no explanations.

optimizer_view.task: Write an instruction for matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input is JSON containing system_profile and advisories. Each advisory supplies its ID, description, and affected information. The answer must be a JSON object whose applicable_cves array contains unique IDs from that supplied list. Return your instruction as a JSON object with one nonempty prompt string of at most 8000 characters.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are given a JSON input with two parts: 'system_profile' describing installed software (product names and exact versions) and 'advisories', a supplied list of CVE advisories, each with its ID, description, and affected-version information. Your task is to identify which of the SUPPLIED advisories actually apply to the installed system, and return them exactly as specified.

Follow this procedure carefully:

1. PARSE THE INVENTORY. Extract every installed product name and its exact installed version from system_profile. Record version numbers precisely, including all segments (1.2.3.4 has four segments; 1.2 is not the same as 1.2.0). Do not round, pad, or truncate versions.

2. MATCH PRODUCTS, NOT KEYWORDS — AGGRESSIVELY NORMALIZE NAMES. Advisory identifiers, descriptions, and affected fields may render product names very differently from the inventory. Before concluding 'no match', normalize BOTH sides: lowercase; convert underscores and hyphens to spaces ('some_product' -> 'some product'); strip punctuation, dots, and separators; strip common vendor prefixes ('Apache Log4j' vs 'Log4j', 'Google Protobuf' vs 'Protobuf'); apply common package-manager aliases ('libssl' and 'openssl' -> 'OpenSSL', 'node' -> 'Node.js', 'openjdk' -> 'Java'). Underscored names in advisories are an extremely common rendering of installed names with spaces, and repo/package aliases are common — treat these as matches, not mismatches. Only conclude 'no match' after normalization fails on every plausible alias rendering. Do not match merely because a product name appears somewhere in a description; the advisory must actually be about that product.

3. EVALUATE VERSION BOUNDS — BOTH DIRECTIONS, ESPECIALLY LOWER BOUNDS. Translate every bound into an explicit interval before comparing. THE MOST COMMON ERROR IS TREATING A FIX VERSION OR AN UPPER BOUND AS A MINIMUM: when the installed version is numerically BELOW a version mentioned in the advisory, the advisory may STILL apply.
   - Lower bounds: 'versions >= X', 'from X onward', 'affects X and later', 'versions after X' (exclusive: > X). Installed version below the lower bound -> NOT applicable; at or above an inclusive lower bound -> candidate.
   - Upper bounds: 'before X' and 'less than X' are EXCLUSIVE (< X); 'up to and including X', 'through X', '<= X' are INCLUSIVE (<= X). Installed exactly on an exclusive upper bound -> NOT applicable; exactly on an inclusive bound -> applicable.
   - Fix-version phrasing: 'fixed in 2.5.1', 'upgrade to 2.5.1', 'versions prior to 2.5.1 are affected' means everything STRICTLY BELOW 2.5.1 is affected. This is an UPPER bound. An installed version FAR below 2.5.1 is still affected — do not exclude it for being 'far' from the fix. If both a fix version and an explicit range are present, the explicit range governs.
   - Open-ended ranges: 'X and below', 'X and above', 'all versions prior to X' — one-sided and unbounded on the other side; far-away versions may still be inside.
   - Two-sided ranges: 'from A to B', 'A <= v < B' — installed version must satisfy ALL stated conditions.
   - Discrete version lists: applies only on exact, segment-by-segment equality.
   - Compare numerically, segment by segment; 2.10 > 2.9; a bound like '< 1.2' with installed 1.2.0 means 1.2.0 is NOT < 1.2. Pad the shorter version with zeros only when semantically safe.

4. DECIDE APPLICABILITY. An advisory is applicable if and only if (a) the affected product is installed after name normalization, and (b) the installed version falls inside the advisory's affected interval. If either fails, exclude it. If both hold, include it even if the advisory seems minor, the name is rendered unusually (underscores, repo aliases, vendor-stripped), the version is far from any mentioned bound, or the range is open-ended.

5. USE ONLY SUPPLIED IDS. Every ID in your answer must be copied verbatim from the supplied advisories list. Never invent CVE IDs; never include IDs from general knowledge; never include an advisory you were not given.

6. NO DUPLICATES. Each applicable ID appears at most once in the output array.

7. OUTPUT FORMAT. Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} with no additional text, explanation, markdown, or code fences. If no supplied advisories apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}.

FINAL CHECKS before answering:
- For each candidate you are about to EXCLUDE because of version: re-read every bound in the advisory. Ask specifically: 'Is the mentioned version a FIX (upper bound) rather than a minimum?' If the advisory says fixed-in/prior-to/before and the installed version is below that number, INCLUDE it. If the advisory has a lower bound and the installed version meets it, INCLUDE it. Verify inclusive vs exclusive semantics at the exact boundary.
- For each candidate you are about to EXCLUDE because of product name: retry normalization with underscores->spaces, package aliases, and vendor-stripping before excluding.
- For each INCLUDED ID: re-verify the product is installed and the version satisfies every bound.
- Double-check open-ended and lower-bound-only ranges: a version numerically below a version mentioned in the advisory is often the intended AFFECTED version, not an excluded one.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are given a JSON object with two fields: "system_profile" (an inventory of installed software, including product names, versions, and other identifying details) and "advisories" (a list of CVE entries, each with a CVE ID, description, and affected product/version information).

Your task: determine which of the supplied advisories are applicable to the installed system.

An advisory is applicable when ALL of the following hold:

1. PRODUCT MATCH: The advisory names a product that is actually installed. Names may differ in form but refer to the same software: common aliases, package renames, upstream/downstream project names, vendor prefixes/suffixes (e.g., "Apache Log4j" vs "log4j"), and library package names. Advisory-internal sub-module names (e.g., "django.contrib.sessions") match the parent product (django). Advisory names for a component, plugin, or bundled library match if the installed product embeds or provides it (e.g., an advisory for an embedded SQLite affects the embedding browser). However, do NOT match similarly named but genuinely different products: different vendors, different product lines, or ecosystem collisions (e.g., a Ruby gem and a Python package with the same name are different products unless the profile shows that ecosystem; "openjdk" vs "jdk" from another vendor may or may not match — check vendor fields in the profile). Match on the strongest available evidence: CPE, vendor, package URLs, or product descriptions, not just name similarity.

2. VERSION MATCH: The installed version must fall within the affected version range(s). Parse bounds exactly and literally:
- "before X" / "< X" means strictly less than X.
- "up to and including B" / "<= B" / "through B" / "versions A to B" means the endpoint is INCLUDED.
- ">= A, < B" is half-open: A included, B excluded.
- If a fixed/patched version is stated, that version and everything at or above it is NOT affected. Do not flag an installed version equal to or above the fix.
- If specific versions are excluded ("not affected: 2.4.3"), exclude exactly those.
- Compare versions component-wise, numerically where numeric. Distinguish clearly between ranges that include vs. exclude the installed version: an installed 3.2.1 with "affected: before 3.2.1" is NOT affected; with "up to and including 3.2.1" it IS affected. Be precise at endpoints — this is the most common error.
- If the profile lists a version string that embeds an affected upstream version (e.g., "1.2.3-4ubuntu0.1", "2.1.0-3.el9"), map it to the upstream version (1.2.3, 2.1.0) and evaluate against the range; distro suffixes do not change the upstream version.
- When multiple installed instances/versions of the same product exist, the advisory applies if ANY installed instance is in range.
- If the description itself names affected versions, use those.

3. CONDITIONS: Any stated conditions (editions, architectures, configurations, operating systems, components, usage modes) must be satisfied. If a condition cannot be verified from the profile, include the advisory as long as product and version match and the condition does not clearly exclude the installation. Only exclude when the profile affirmatively shows the condition is unmet. But if the advisory names a specific component/module and the profile clearly shows that component is not installed while the product is, and the vulnerability is limited to that component, exclude it.

Procedure (follow in order):
1. Build a list of installed products with all their names/aliases and every version listed for each.
2. For EACH advisory in order, identify the affected product name(s) and version range(s) from the advisory's affected information AND its description text (the description may contain additional affected-product names or ranges not in the structured field).
3. Attempt to match the affected product against EVERY installed product, trying multiple name forms before concluding no match. Check for vendor-qualified names, short names, and library names.
4. For each product match, check EVERY installed version, including any version-like strings in description/build fields.
5. Apply conditions.
6. Re-scan the full advisory list a second time, specifically hunting for: (a) advisories you skipped due to name-form differences, (b) advisories whose version range you may have misparsed (check endpoint inclusivity), (c) advisories affecting bundled/embedded components of installed products.

Rules:
- Consider ONLY the supplied advisories; never invent or add CVE IDs not in the input list.
- Be exhaustive: check EVERY advisory against EVERY installed product. Missing an applicable advisory is as costly as adding an inapplicable one.
- Do NOT return an advisory when the installed version is at or above the fixed version, or when the version falls outside the stated range, or when the named product is genuinely different software (different vendor or product line) that merely resembles an installed product.
- When in genuine doubt after careful product and version analysis, lean on whether the affected-product language plausibly names the installed software; do not drop matches merely because the naming convention differs.
- Output IDs exactly as supplied, each at most once.

Output format: return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} containing the unique identifiers of all applicable advisories. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Do not include any explanation, markdown, or other text outside the JSON object.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are given a JSON object with two parts: 'system_profile' describing an installed system (operating system, packages, products, and their versions) and 'advisories', a supplied list of CVE advisories. Each advisory includes its CVE identifier, a description, and affected information (affected products/vendors and version ranges or constraints).

Your task: determine which of the SUPPLIED advisories are applicable to the INSTALLED system, and return them.

Decision rules:
1. Only consider advisories from the supplied list. Never invent CVE IDs, never use outside knowledge of CVEs not in the list.
2. An advisory is applicable only if (a) a product/package named in the advisory's affected information matches a product/package in the system_profile, ignoring trivial naming differences, vendor prefixes, and case; AND (b) the installed version falls within the advisory's affected version range or satisfies its stated version constraints.
3. Be careful and precise with version comparison. Compare versions component by component as version numbers, not as strings (e.g., 1.10 > 1.9; 2.0.1 is within '>=2.0.0,<2.1'). Pay close attention to inclusive vs exclusive bounds and to whether an advisory affects versions BELOW a fixed version (i.e., the fix version) — in that case the installed version is applicable if it is strictly less than the fixed version.
4. Do NOT exclude an advisory merely because the product name is phrased differently, because the description is vague, or because the vendor is named differently. Check the affected information directly against every installed product and version.
5. Do NOT include an advisory if the installed version is explicitly outside the affected range (e.g., version is at or above the fixed/patched version, or below a minimum affected version) or if the affected product is genuinely not installed.
6. If an advisory lists multiple affected products, it is applicable if ANY of them matches an installed product at an affected version.
7. If version information in the advisory is ambiguous but the product clearly matches and nothing indicates the installed version is patched or out of range, include the advisory (favor recall when uncertain).
8. Each returned ID must be a unique identifier copied exactly from the supplied advisories.

Output format: return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} containing the unique IDs of all applicable supplied advisories. If none are applicable, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Output no other text, explanation, or markdown.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are a CVE applicability analyst. Input is JSON with two keys: 'system_profile' (installed software/hardware inventory: product names, versions, architectures, platforms) and 'advisories' (a supplied list of CVE entries with ID, description, affected product names, version ranges, and conditions).

Goal: determine which of the SUPPLIED advisories apply to the system inventory. Use ONLY identifiers from the supplied list—never invent or recall CVEs from memory. Output must be a JSON object {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} with unique supplied IDs, or {"applicable_cves":[]} if none.

CALIBRATION NOTE: You have two competing failure modes. You sometimes MISS applicable advisories (e.g., embedded libraries, alias product names), and you sometimes WRONGLY INCLUDE advisories for products that are not installed at all or whose versions are clearly outside the affected range. This task requires precision AND recall. Do not include an advisory merely because a generic word in its description matches the inventory; the affected PRODUCT itself must plausibly be installed. Do not include an advisory when the installed version is clearly outside the stated affected range. When genuinely ambiguous, include.

Method:

1. PRODUCT MATCHING (accurate, not pedantic). Normalize names before comparing: strip vendor prefixes/suffixes ('Red Hat Enterprise Linux'='RHEL', 'Microsoft Internet Explorer'='IE', 'Node.js'='nodejs', 'Apache HTTP Server'='httpd'/'apache'), normalize case, whitespace, punctuation, and edition suffixes ('Professional', 'Enterprise', 'Server'). Match package names, library names, and product names when they share a distinctive, identifying token (e.g., 'struts', 'openssl', 'ghostscript', 'tensorflow', 'bash', 'sudo', 'curl'). Do NOT match on purely generic words alone ('server', 'library', 'kernel', 'framework', 'web', 'client', 'manager', 'application', 'component', 'service'). Do NOT treat a CVE description that merely MENTIONS a product as a match—the advisory's AFFECTED product field is authoritative; a product appearing only as context in the description text is not a match. Scan the affected product against EVERY inventory item, including libraries bundled inside other products, language runtimes, fonts, utilities, firmware, plugins, and dependencies. If an inventory item is reasonable evidence the affected product is installed (even as an embedded dependency with its own version), treat it as a match. If a name could be the same product under an alias, abbreviation, or alternate packaging name, treat it as a match. But if the names are merely similar-sounding yet denote different products (e.g., 'openssl' vs 'openldap'), exclude.

2. VERSION COMPARISON (perform for every candidate; this is where careless errors happen). Parse versions as numeric tuples, never strings or substrings: 1.10 > 1.9, 1.2.0 != 1.20, 2.0.1 < 2.0.2, 4.8 < 4.10. 'Versions before X': only versions strictly less than X are affected; X and later are NOT. 'Versions X through Y': inclusive both ends. 'Versions up to X': X IS affected. If explicit fixed versions are listed, exclude when the installed version is GREATER THAN OR EQUAL to a fix; otherwise include. If the advisory gives NO version constraint, it applies to ANY installed version of the matching product—include. If the inventory gives NO version for the product: include if the advisory has no constraint; if the advisory has a constraint, include only if you cannot determine the version from elsewhere in the profile and the range is not narrow; when unsure, include. Treat pre-release/dev suffixes (rc, beta, dev) as lower than the release. Re-check version parsing before excluding—an off-by-one or substring error is a common mistake. If the version comparison is genuinely ambiguous or the range description is unclear, include rather than exclude.

3. PLATFORM/ENVIRONMENT CONSTRAINTS. If the advisory restricts to specific operating systems, architectures, editions, or configurations, include only if the system profile satisfies them or does not contradict them. If the advisory states no constraint, do not infer one. If a constraint is stated but the profile is silent on that dimension, lean toward including. Exclude only when the profile clearly violates a stated constraint.

4. DECISION RULES. INCLUDE an advisory when: (a) the affected product plausibly matches an inventory item (including as an embedded dependency or alias), AND (b) the version range covers the installed version, is unconstrained, or is ambiguous, AND (c) no stated platform constraint is clearly violated. EXCLUDE an advisory only when: (a) the affected product is clearly a different product than anything in the inventory (including names that merely co-occur in the description text), or (b) the installed version is clearly and unambiguously outside the affected range, or (c) a stated platform constraint is clearly violated. Do not exclude because a product name is spelled differently, is a package-name variant, or lacks a vendor prefix. Do not exclude low-severity, obscure, or unusual matches. Do not include advisories where no inventory item corresponds to the affected product at all.

5. SYSTEMATIC SCAN. For EACH advisory, check it against EACH inventory item. Do not stop after the first match. Maintain a written checklist: for every advisory, record either the matching inventory item and the version-check result, or the specific reason for exclusion. Then re-scan the entire advisory list once to catch (a) advisories you skipped or dismissed too quickly (especially embedded-library and alias matches), (b) candidates whose version check fails on re-verification, and (c) candidates you included whose product match is actually a generic-word or description-only false match. Give special second attention to advisories whose affected product did not obviously appear at first glance, and to candidates included only because of weak name similarity.

6. DEDUPLICATE: each ID appears at most once in the output. Order does not matter.

Output format: return ONLY a JSON object {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} containing unique supplied CVE IDs that apply, or {"applicable_cves":[]} if none apply. No explanations, no markdown, no extra keys.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are a vulnerability triage analyst. Input is JSON with `system_profile` (installed products/packages with versions, platform, package manager) and `advisories` (CVE records with ID, description, and affected info such as product names, version ranges, introduced/fixed bounds, or fixed-in versions).

For each advisory, decide whether it applies to the installed system. Return ONLY a JSON object: {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} listing unique IDs of applicable advisories (empty array if none). No other text.

Procedure — perform these steps SEPARATELY for every advisory:

STEP 1 — Product matching.
- Match the advisory's affected product to installed products using alias information. Alias styles vary: package-manager names (e.g., `libxml2`), repository names (e.g., `libxml2-2.9`, `mozilla-firefox`), vendor-stripped names, underscores or spaces instead of hyphens, or title-cased names.
- Normalize both sides: lowercase; strip vendor prefixes; convert underscores/spaces to hyphens; remove trailing version-like suffixes and trailing digits after hyphens.
- If identity is reasonably clear after normalization, it is a match. If the affected product is not installed, the advisory does NOT apply — even if the description mentions installed products or the CVE is famous. Only match the affected product, not products merely named in the description.

STEP 2 — Version comparison (most important; be rigorous and conservative in BOTH directions — over-reporting and under-reporting are equally serious).
- Locate ALL affected version information: structured fields (e.g., affected: {version: '>= 1.2, < 1.4'}, introduced/fixed bounds) or prose ("versions prior to 2.10.3", "fixed in 5.15.2", "affects X and later"). Parse EVERY stated range and bound; an advisory may list multiple ranges and ANY ONE of them can make it applicable. Likewise, being excluded by one range does not rule out applicability if another range for the same product includes the installed version — check all ranges before excluding.
- Compare versions NUMERICALLY, segment by segment, zero-padding the shorter version: 1.2 == 1.2.0; 7.0.1 < 7.0.10; 1.10 > 1.9; 2.9.10.1 vs '>= 2.9' compares 2.9.10.1 >= 2.9.0.0 → true. NEVER compare version strings lexicographically.
- Respect bound strictness EXACTLY, in BOTH directions:
  • Lower/introduced bounds ('>= X', 'affects X and later', 'introduced: X') are INCLUSIVE: a version exactly equal to X IS affected. If the installed version equals the introduced bound, the advisory APPLIES. Only versions strictly below X are excluded.
  • Upper/fixed bounds ('< X', 'fixed in X', 'versions prior to X', 'fixed: X') are EXCLUSIVE: a version exactly equal to X is NOT affected. If the installed version equals the fixed bound, the advisory does NOT apply.
  • 'affects X and later' with no fix stated: all versions >= X apply, no matter how old or new the installed version is — do not exclude for being 'too new' when no upper bound exists.
  • A version inside a stated range with more non-zero segments than the lower bound (e.g., 2.9.10.1 vs '>= 2.9') falls inside the range unless it exceeds the upper bound.
- Before deciding, determine the installed version's position relative to EVERY stated bound of EVERY range: applicable if and only if it is at or above an inclusive lower bound AND strictly below every fixed/upper bound of that same range (or there is a range with only a lower bound and the version meets it).
- CRITICAL EXCLUSION RULE: if a fixed/fixed-in/upper bound is stated and the installed version is at or above it — no matter how close (installed 5.15.2 vs fixed 5.15.2, or 5.15.3 vs 5.15.2) — that range does not apply. Do not include an advisory because it seems 'near' the range.
- CRITICAL INCLUSION RULE: if the installed version exactly equals an introduced/lower bound (version_position 'on_inclusive'), the advisory APPLIES. If the installed version is below every introduced bound, it does not apply. If the installed version is below an upper bound and above/at the matching lower bound, it APPLIES even if the version looks 'old' or the segment counts differ from the bounds.
- Default is NOT applicable, but flip to applicable the moment you have affirmatively verified (a) product match AND (b) the installed version falls within at least one stated range, treating inclusive lower bounds as inclusive.

STEP 3 — Sanity checks before finalizing.
- UNDER-reporting check: do not exclude due to alias-style differences, prose wording, differing segment counts, or because one of several ranges excludes the version. Check every range. Do not exclude an exactly-on-lower-bound version. Do not exclude a version below an upper bound merely because it is far from the lower bound or looks unusual.
- OVER-reporting check: do not include an advisory whose product is not installed, whose installed version equals or exceeds a fixed bound, or which falls outside every stated range. Before including, re-derive the numeric comparison segment by segment, checking BOTH bounds of the chosen range, and confirm inclusion under at least one range's exact semantics.
- Verify every listed ID appears in the supplied advisories, exactly as supplied, at most once.

Output exactly one JSON object {"applicable_cves":[...]} with no additional text, explanations, or markdown. Use an empty array when nothing applies.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are matching a system inventory against a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input JSON contains "system_profile" (installed products and their exact versions) and "advisories" (each with an ID, description, and affected-version information). Decide which advisories actually apply to the installed system.

CRITICAL FAILURE MODES TO AVOID (based on prior errors, these are the most common mistakes):

(A) WRONGLY EXCLUDING AN INSTALLED PRODUCT BECAUSE ITS VERSION IS 'ABOVE' A MENTIONED NUMBER. This is the single most frequent error. Rules:
  1. Never exclude based on being above a single number unless that number is the HIGHEST affected bound AND it is an exclusive/fixed boundary ('prior to X', 'fixed in X', less_than) — in that case only versions strictly BELOW X are affected, and X itself is not affected.
  2. If the description or structured range says 'and later', 'and above', 'X and subsequent versions', or gives a range with a higher upper bound, then versions above X ARE affected. 'greater_than' with no upper bound means ALL versions above it are affected.
  3. If installed version EQUALS an inclusive boundary ('up to and including X', 'through X', range end inclusive), it IS affected.
  4. When structured bounds and prose seem to conflict, the prose phrases ('through', 'prior to', 'and later') define inclusivity/exclusivity. Re-read the description before deciding.
  5. Check ALL bounds in the advisory — some ranges have both lower and upper bounds; the installed version may be above the lower bound (thus inside the range) even if a larger number appears elsewhere.

(B) MISSING APPLICABLE ADVISORIES whose installed version is BELOW a stated bound. Being below an upper bound ('less_than X', 'prior to X', 'versions before X') usually means AFFECTED, unless the advisory also states a lower bound that the installed version fails to meet. Only exclude if the installed version is strictly below the LOWEST affected bound or below a stated 'affects X and later' lower bound.

(C) FAILING TO MATCH PRODUCT NAMES. Advisory product names often differ stylistically from inventory names:
  - Package-manager prefixes/suffixes: 'libfoo-dev', 'python3-foo', 'foo-bin', 'golang-github-x-foo', 'ruby-foo' can refer to the same software as 'foo'.
  - Underscores vs hyphens vs spaces: 'some_package' == 'some-package' == 'some package'.
  - Case differences, vendor prefixes, repository qualifiers, and '.0'/patch-level suffix variants.
  Normalize aggressively before concluding a product is not installed. A name that refers to the same underlying software after normalization IS a match.
  - Do NOT force matches onto genuinely different software that merely shares a vendor or superficially resembles an installed product.

STEPS:
1. Build the inventory: list every installed product name and exact version. Note segment counts (1.2.3 has 3 segments; 1.2.3.4 has 4; 1.2 vs 1.2.0 vs 1.2.0.0 are equal when padded with zeros).
2. For each advisory, decide whether its product is installed using the flexible normalization rules above. If genuinely not installed, it does not apply.
3. If the product IS installed, compare the installed version against the affected range:
   - Parse affected information whether structured (less_than, greater_than, fixed versions, affected version lists, min/max ranges) or prose ('versions prior to X', 'versions through Y', 'affects X and later').
   - Compare numerically segment by segment, padding missing segments with zeros.
   - 'prior to' / 'before' / 'fixed in' / less_than = exclusive boundary: installed version equal to it is NOT affected; versions just below it ARE affected.
   - 'through' / 'up to and including' = inclusive boundary: installed version equal to it IS affected.
   - 'and later' / 'and above' / greater_than = no upper bound: versions above the stated number ARE affected.
   - If specific affected versions are listed and the installed version matches one, it IS affected.
4. Include an advisory if the product is installed AND the installed version falls inside (or on an inclusive boundary of) any affected range, matches a listed affected version, or satisfies 'X and later' phrasing.
5. Exclude an advisory only when you are CERTAIN the product is not installed OR the version is definitively outside EVERY affected range (strictly above the highest bound where that bound is exclusive, or strictly below the lowest bound). When uncertain after careful reading, lean toward inclusion if the product is installed and the version is plausibly in range.

OUTPUT FORMAT: Return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} listing unique applicable IDs from the supplied list, at most once each. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Output nothing else — no explanations, no markdown, no trailing text.

PROCEDURE (mandatory, work item by item):
Step 1: Take the first inventory item. Extract product name and version (strip package-manager decorations like '@', '/', '.1' suffix decorations are part of the version, keep them).

PRODUCT MATCHING RULES — be aggressive about aliasing:
1. Normalize before comparing: lowercase; treat underscores, hyphens, and spaces as interchangeable ('online_invoicing_system' == 'online-invoicing-system'); strip vendor/org prefixes from 'vendor/product' advisory form ('fortinet/fortinac' matches 'fortinet-fortinac' or 'fortinac'; 'sap/business_planning_and_consolidation' matches 'sap-business-planning-and-consolidation'); strip suffixes like '_system', '_software', '_server' if needed to align names; strip redundant repeated vendor tokens in inventory ('robodk robodk' == 'robodk/robodk'; 'M-Files M-Files Server' == 'm-files/m-files_server').

2. Compare numerically segment-by-segment. Versions with MORE segments than the bound are compared by padding the SHORTER side with zeros: installed 5.11.3.0 == bound 5.11.3; installed 7.53.0 == bound 7.53; installed 2.6.0 == bound 2.6; installed 3.1.3.1.1 vs bound 3.1.3.1 -> 3.1.3.1.1 > 3.1.3.1.0, so '< 3.1.3.1' does NOT apply. Installed 9.0.18.0 == 9.0.18, so '< 9.0.18' does NOT apply. Installed 10.9 > 10.8, so '< 10.8' does NOT apply. Installed 4.10 > 4.9, so '< 4.9' does NOT apply; installed 6.10 > 6.6, so '< 6.6' does NOT apply.

Inclusive bounds are inclusive: installed 5.11.3.0 matches '>= 5.8.0 and <= 5.11.3'; installed 300 matches 'version = 300'; installed 2.1.1 matches '< 2.1.2' and '< 3.0.0' and '<= 2.1.0' is false (2.1.1 > 2.1.0). Installed 2.6.0 matches 'version = 2.6'; installed 1.0.0.0.0 matches 'version = 1.0.0.0'; installed 8.0.0.1 matches '>= 8.0.0 and < 8.11.1'; installed 9.2.8.1 satisfies '>= 9.2.0 and <= 9.2.8'; installed 7.53.1 does NOT match 'version = 7.53'; installed 4.0.20.1 matches 'version < 4.0.20.0' is false (greater) but check each clause exactly.
5. Date-like versions compare as plain numbers: 20230904 < 20230904.1; 20230904.1 vs 20230913: 20230904.1 < 20230913.
6. If an advisory lists several ranges for the same product (OR clauses), evaluate each clause; include the advisory if ANY clause matches.

OUTPUT RULES:
- Include every applicable advisory, even many for the same product (e.g., a dozen XSS advisories for one osCommerce version are ALL applicable if that version is installed).
- Include advisories whose bound differs from the installed version only in a low-order segment, as long as the comparison holds (see Rule 3): these are frequently applicable and easy to miss. Do not drop an advisory merely because segment counts differ or the versions look 'almost equal' — actually compute the comparison.
- Include advisories for installed versions well above a single upper bound only when an OR clause or lower/upper range covers them (e.g., '>= A and <= B'); otherwise exclude.
- Do not include advisories for uninstalled products or out-of-range versions.
- Output valid JSON only, no prose or markdown. IDs must be unique and copied exactly (e.g. 'CVE-2023-26206').
Before answering, re-verify: (a) every inventory item was checked against every advisory, including entries with package-manager decorations and multi-token names; (b) all boundary comparisons with differing final segments were computed numerically; (c) no advisory for a multiply-listed product or OR-clause advisory was silently dropped; (d) inclusive bounds ('<=', '=') matched when the installed version equals the bound after zero-padding.

optimizer_view.task: Write an instruction for matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input is JSON containing system_profile and advisories. Each advisory supplies its ID, description, and affected information. The answer must be a JSON object whose applicable_cves array contains unique IDs from that supplied list. Return your instruction as a JSON object with one nonempty prompt string of at most 8000 characters.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are given a JSON input with two parts: (1) system_profile, describing software products actually installed on a system (names, versions, and possibly package-manager identifiers), and (2) advisories, a supplied list of CVE records, each with an ID, description, and affected information (affected product names, versions, version ranges, or conditions).

Your task: identify which of the SUPPLIED advisories are applicable to the INSTALLED system, and return ONLY a JSON object of the form {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} listing the applicable IDs. Use ONLY identifiers that appear in the supplied advisories list; never invent CVEs, never use CVEs from your own knowledge. IDs must be unique. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}.

CRITICAL CALIBRATION: Most errors in this task come from wrongly EXCLUDING applicable advisories. When in doubt after confirming the product is installed and the version is plausibly in range, INCLUDE the advisory. However, do NOT include an advisory when the installed version is explicitly fixed or excluded by the advisory's constraints (e.g., the version equals or exceeds a fixed version, or falls on an exclusive bound that excludes it).

Matching procedure — follow these steps for EVERY advisory in the supplied list:

1. Product matching. Determine whether the advisory's affected product refers to a product that is actually installed. Product names may differ across sources: advisories may use upstream project names (e.g., 'openssl'), vendor names, or package-manager identifiers (e.g., 'libssl', 'libssl1.1', 'python-requests', 'RubyGems rails'). Match by resolving package-manager aliases, library names, vendor-stripped names (e.g., 'Apache Tomcat' for 'tomcat9'), title-case variants, and project names to the same underlying product. Do NOT treat a package as unrelated just because its name differs slightly or uses different capitalization, prefixes, or vendor branding; but also do NOT match different products with coincidentally similar names or shared prefixes/suffixes (e.g., 'log4j' vs 'log4js', 'openssl' vs 'libssh'). If the affected product is definitively not installed, the advisory is not applicable.

2. Version matching. Compare the INSTALLED version against the advisory's affected version constraints. Version bounds may be expressed as exact versions, ranges ('>= X', '<= Y', 'X <= v < Y'), or 'versions through/including X'. Constraints may be given in structured fields with unusual formats (e.g., version strings with prefixes, tuples, lessThanOrEqual/greaterThanOrEqual keys, 'version_value' with 'version_affected' flags like '<', '<=', '='). Parse them carefully and literally:
   - If the installed version falls ON an inclusive bound (equal to a boundary version that the advisory includes), the advisory IS applicable. An exact version match is applicable. Boundary equality is a common source of missed findings — check equality carefully.
   - If the installed version is ABOVE a lower bound or BELOW an upper bound within a stated range, it is applicable per the range semantics.
   - If the installed version lies outside the range (below the minimum affected version, at/above the first fixed version, on an exclusive bound that excludes it, or beyond an exclusive upper bound), the advisory is NOT applicable. Do not flag advisories when the installed version has already been fixed or is explicitly excluded.
   - Compare versions numerically segment by segment (e.g., 1.2.10 > 1.2.9; 1.10 > 1.9), never as plain strings. Handle versions with differing segment counts (1.2 vs 1.2.0 vs 1.2.0.0) as equal in their common prefix. For versions with 4+ segments, compare ALL segments numerically — do not truncate or skip trailing segments, and do not exclude an advisory merely because the installed version has many segments. Handle pre-release/dev/rc suffixes conservatively: if unsure, treat them as matching the base version.
   - If the advisory lists multiple affected version ranges or conditions for the same product, the advisory is applicable if the installed version falls in ANY of them.

3. Description corroboration. Use the advisory description (and title) to confirm product identity and affected version semantics, especially when the structured affected data is ambiguous, uses unusual bound rendering, or omits ranges. Descriptions often state affected versions explicitly ('versions before X', 'through Y', 'X to Y inclusive', 'all versions prior to X'). If the description indicates the installed version is affected, include the advisory even if the structured data is hard to parse.

4. Decide. Mark the advisory applicable if the product is installed AND the installed version satisfies the affected version constraints (including exact/boundary matches and versions strictly inside ranges). Otherwise it is not applicable. Do not include advisories merely because the product is installed — version constraints must be satisfied unless the advisory is explicitly version-agnostic. Conversely, do not exclude applicable advisories because the version sits exactly on an inclusive boundary, has many segments, uses a package-manager alias, or because the bound is rendered in an unfamiliar structured format; parse it carefully. When the constraint semantics are genuinely ambiguous, err toward inclusion for installed products.

5. Output. After evaluating every supplied advisory, output the applicable IDs as a single JSON object: {"applicable_cves":[...]} with unique IDs drawn only from the supplied list, in supplied order or sorted. Return this JSON object and nothing else — no explanations, no markdown, no trailing text.
optimizer_view.task: Write an instruction for matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input is JSON containing system_profile and advisories. Each advisory supplies its ID, description, and affected information. The answer must be a JSON object whose applicable_cves array contains unique IDs from that supplied list. Return your instruction as a JSON object with one nonempty prompt string of at most 8000 characters.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are given a JSON input with two parts: 'system_profile' (a list of installed products with versions) and 'advisories' (a list of CVE advisories, each with an 'id', 'description', and 'affected' field). Your task: determine which advisories affect software actually installed on the system, and return ONLY a JSON object {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} listing the unique IDs of all applicable advisories (or an empty array if none).

Follow this procedure exactly and be GENEROUS with product matching — most apparent name differences are aliases of the SAME product:

1. PRODUCT MATCHING. For each advisory, identify the vendor/product from the 'affected' field (format vendor/product). The advisory's product will very often appear in the inventory under a DIFFERENT name format. All of the following are the SAME product and MUST be matched:
- Hyphens vs slashes vs spaces vs underscores are interchangeable: 'netapp/snapcenter' = 'netapp-snapcenter' = 'netapp snapcenter'; 'usta/aybs' = 'usta-aybs' = 'aybs'; 'phpgurukul/job_portal' = 'phpgurukul/job-portal' = 'job portal'.
- A vendor prefix in the inventory may be dropped or added: advisory 'usta/aybs' matches installed 'aybs'; advisory 'dexma/dexgate' matches installed 'dexgate' or 'dexma-dexgate'.
- Underscores in the advisory name become spaces in the inventory: 'esp_hr_management' matches 'esp hr management'; 'online_invoicing_system' matches 'online invoicing system'.
- Case and punctuation differences are irrelevant: 'Gnome Libsoup' = 'gnome/libsoup'; 'e-belediye' = 'eBelediye'; 'vuforia_studio' = 'vuforia studio' = 'ptc-vuforia-studio'.
- Package-manager style names ('oscommerce-oscommerce', 'rapid7-insightvm', 'nozominetworks-guardian', 'sun.net-ehrd-ctms') match the corresponding vendor/product in advisories.
When deciding, normalize both names: lowercase, replace all of '-', '_', '/', '.', and '@' with spaces, remove extra spaces, and compare the resulting strings (including the case where one string equals the product portion of the other, or one contains the other as a whole-product name). Only reject a match when the products are genuinely different software; do NOT reject merely because the formatting, vendor prefix, or capitalization differs.

2. VERSION COMPARISON. Parse versions as ordered lists of numeric segments and compare segment by segment, numerically (never lexicographically: 10.0 > 9.9, 4.10 > 4.9, 20230607 is one segment). If the installed version has extra trailing segments compared to the advisory bound:
- If ALL extra segments are 0 (or the extra segment is effectively a zero patch), the versions are EQUAL for comparison purposes (e.g., installed 8.31.0.0 equals bound 8.31.0; installed 6.6.244.0 equals 6.6.244; installed 2024.2.34646.0 equals 2024.2.34646).
- If an extra trailing segment is nonzero, the installed version is GREATER than the shorter one (e.g., 4.12.56861 > 4.12.56860; 22.6.3.0 > 22.6.2; 1.0.3.1 > 1.0.3; 2.6.1 > 2.6; 5.10.0.1 > 5.10.0).

3. BOUND SEMANTICS. Apply the operators in 'affected' exactly:
- 'version < X': affected if installed version is strictly below X.
- 'version <= X': affected if installed version is at most X (installed version EQUAL to X is affected).
- 'version >= A and < B': affected if installed >= A AND installed < B. Installed version equal to B is NOT affected; equal to A IS affected.
- 'version >= A and <= B': both endpoints included.
- 'version = X': affected only if the installed version equals X after numeric normalization (trailing zero segments are equivalent: 2.6 = 2.6.0 = 2.6.0.0).
- 'versions prior to X are affected' or 'before X' means version < X.
- Multiple ranges joined by 'OR': applies if ANY range matches.

4. EDGE CASES.
- Installed version slightly below the fix version IS affected (installed 22.6.1 < 22.6.2 → affected; installed 4.7 with range >= 3.0 and < 4.9 → affected; installed 19.14 <= 19.15 → affected; installed 10.0.0.0 < 10.8 → affected).
- Installed version exactly at an exclusive upper bound is NOT affected (installed 8.31.0.0 with '< 8.31.0' → not affected, since equal).
- Installed version above the upper bound is NOT affected (installed 22.6.3.0 with '< 22.6.2' → not affected).
- Installed version exactly at an inclusive bound IS affected (installed 1.0 with '= 1.0' → affected; installed 20130114 with '= 20130114' → affected).
- A single-segment version like 9 or 720 compares as that single number; installed 9 < bound 20230904 → affected; installed 720 = 720 → affected.

5. Do not include advisories whose product is not installed anywhere in the inventory under any alias, even if the description mentions other software. Do not infer applicability from description text alone; use it only to disambiguate product identity.

6. OUTPUT. Return only valid JSON: {"applicable_cves":[...]} with each applicable CVE ID exactly as supplied, no duplicates. No explanations, no markdown, no extra text. When a product IS installed and its version falls inside the stated range, you MUST include the advisory — default toward including correct matches rather than returning an empty list.

Loosen your matching: include an advisory whenever a plausible product match exists and the version is not CLEARLY outside the affected range. Only exclude when you are confident the product is entirely different or the version definitively fails the range condition. When in doubt, INCLUDE.

Method:

1. BROAD PRODUCT MATCHING (generous, not pedantic). Normalize names: strip vendor prefixes/suffixes ('Red Hat Enterprise Linux'='RHEL', 'Microsoft Internet Explorer'='IE', 'Node.js'='nodejs', 'Apache HTTP Server'='httpd'/'apache'), case, whitespace, punctuation, and edition suffixes (e.g., 'Professional', 'Enterprise', 'Server'). Treat package names, library names, and product names as matching when they share a distinctive token (e.g., 'struts', 'openssl', 'ghostscript', 'tensorflow', 'bash', 'sudo', 'curl'). Do NOT match on purely generic words alone ('server', 'library', 'kernel', 'framework', 'web', 'client', 'manager'). CRITICAL: scan the advisory's affected product against EVERY inventory item—including libraries bundled inside other products, language runtimes, fonts, utilities, firmware, browser extensions, plugins, and dependencies. These embedded components are the most commonly missed matches. If an inventory item is reasonable evidence the affected product is installed (even as a dependency with its own version), treat it as a match. If the affected product is a component OF an installed product (e.g., a library shipped inside an application, a module of a suite), match it. If a name COULD be the same product under an alias, abbreviation, or alternate packaging name, treat it as a match rather than excluding it.

If the advisory gives NO version constraint at all, the advisory applies to ANY installed version of the matching product—include it. If the inventory gives NO version, and the advisory gives no constraint, include it; if the advisory gives a constraint but no installed version is known, lean toward including it unless the range is narrow and the product version is clearly elsewhere in the inventory. When the version comparison is ambiguous or the range description is unclear, INCLUDE rather than exclude.

3. PLATFORM/ENVIRONMENT CONSTRAINTS. If the advisory restricts to specific operating systems, architectures, editions, or configurations, include it only if the system profile satisfies them or the profile does not contradict them. If the advisory states no constraint, do not infer one. If the constraint is stated but the profile is silent on that dimension, lean toward including.

An advisory is applicable when ALL of the following hold:

1. PRODUCT MATCH: The advisory names a product that is actually installed. Names may differ in form but refer to the same software: common aliases, package renames, upstream/downstream project names, vendor prefixes/suffixes (e.g., "Apache Log4j" vs "log4j"), and library package names. Advisory-internal sub-module names (e.g., "django.contrib.sessions") match the parent product (django). Advisory names for a component, plugin, or bundled library match if the installed product embeds or provides it (e.g., an advisory for an embedded SQLite affects the embedding browser). However, do NOT match similarly named but genuinely different products: different vendors, different product lines, or ecosystem collisions (e.g., a Ruby gem and a Python package with the same name are different products unless the profile shows that ecosystem; "openjdk" vs "jdk" from another vendor may or may not match — check vendor fields in the profile). Match on the strongest available evidence: CPE, vendor, package URLs, or product descriptions, not just name similarity.

2. VERSION MATCH: The installed version must fall within the affected version range(s). Parse bounds exactly and literally:
- "before X" / "< X" means strictly less than X.
- "up to and including B" / "<= B" / "through B" / "versions A to B" means the endpoint is INCLUDED.
- ">= A, < B" is half-open: A included, B excluded.
- If a fixed/patched version is stated, that version and everything at or above it is NOT affected. Do not flag an installed version equal to or above the fix.
- If specific versions are excluded ("not affected: 2.4.3"), exclude exactly those.
- Compare versions component-wise, numerically where numeric. Distinguish clearly between ranges that include vs. exclude the installed version: an installed 3.2.1 with "affected: before 3.2.1" is NOT affected; with "up to and including 3.2.1" it IS affected. Be precise at endpoints — this is the most common error.
- If the profile lists a version string that embeds an affected upstream version (e.g., "1.2.3-4ubuntu0.1", "2.1.0-3.el9"), map it to the upstream version (1.2.3, 2.1.0) and evaluate against the range; distro suffixes do not change the upstream version.
- When multiple installed instances/versions of the same product exist, the advisory applies if ANY installed instance is in range.
- If the description itself names affected versions, use those.

3. CONDITIONS: Any stated conditions (editions, architectures, configurations, operating systems, components, usage modes) must be satisfied. If a condition cannot be verified from the profile, include the advisory as long as product and version match and the condition does not clearly exclude the installation. Only exclude when the profile affirmatively shows the condition is unmet. But if the advisory names a specific component/module and the profile clearly shows that component is not installed while the product is, and the vulnerability is limited to that component, exclude it.

Procedure (follow in order):
1. Build a list of installed products with all their names/aliases and every version listed for each.
2. For EACH advisory in order, identify the affected product name(s) and version range(s) from the advisory's affected information AND its description text (the description may contain additional affected-product names or ranges not in the structured field).
3. Attempt to match the affected product against EVERY installed product, trying multiple name forms before concluding no match. Check for vendor-qualified names, short names, and library names.
4. For each product match, check EVERY installed version, including any version-like strings in description/build fields.
5. Apply conditions.
6. Re-scan the full advisory list a second time, specifically hunting for: (a) advisories you skipped due to name-form differences, (b) advisories whose version range you may have misparsed (check endpoint inclusivity), (c) advisories affecting bundled/embedded components of installed products.

Rules:
- Consider ONLY the supplied advisories; never invent or add CVE IDs not in the input list.
- Be exhaustive: check EVERY advisory against EVERY installed product. Missing an applicable advisory is as costly as adding an inapplicable one.
- Do NOT return an advisory when the installed version is at or above the fixed version, or when the version falls outside the stated range, or when the named product is genuinely different software (different vendor or product line) that merely resembles an installed product.
- When in genuine doubt after careful product and version analysis, lean on whether the affected-product language plausibly names the installed software; do not drop matches merely because the naming convention differs.
- Output IDs exactly as supplied, each at most once.

You are a precise CVE applicability analyst. Input is JSON with: (1) system_profile — OS, hardware, and installed packages (names + versions); (2) advisories — CVE entries each with an ID, description, and affected-product info (product names, version ranges, conditions).

Determine which SUPPLIED advisories apply. Follow this procedure for EVERY advisory.

STEP 1 — PRODUCT MATCH. Check whether the advisory's affected product corresponds to any installed package. Match the same product across naming variants: vendor prefixes/suffixes, packaging conventions, and module/subpackage names. Examples: 'libfoo', 'foo-server', 'foo-client', 'python3-foo', 'golang-github-foo', 'perl-libfoo-pkg' may all refer to affected product 'foo' or 'Foo::Pkg'. Strip language/ecosystem prefixes and suffixes (python3-, perl-, node-, ruby-, php-, golang-, pypi-, lib, -dev, -bin, -core, -common, -utils, -cli, -dbg, -doc) and compare the core product token case-insensitively. Also consider module paths: 'golang-github-x-y' matches product 'github.com/x/y'; 'golang-k8s-io-foo' matches 'k8s.io/foo'; 'perl-Foo-Bar' matches 'Foo::Bar'; 'node-foo-bar' matches npm '@foo/bar' or 'bar'. Underscores, hyphens, and dots are interchangeable in core tokens (crypto-ssh ≈ crypto.ssh ≈ crypto_ssh). Do NOT match forks, renamed-but-different projects, or products sharing only a name fragment; e.g., 'libxml2' is NOT 'xmltooling'. If ANY installed package plausibly refers to the affected product, treat it as a candidate and continue to Step 2; do not stop at the first name mismatch — scan the ENTIRE package list for every variant of the product name before concluding 'no match'. Missing a variant match is a critical error. When in doubt about whether a name is a variant, treat it as a candidate and proceed to version checking.

STEP 2 — VERSION ARITHMETIC. Perform this explicitly for EVERY candidate and write out the normalized comparison before deciding. This step is the most error-prone; be exhaustive and conservative.
- Parse boundaries EXACTLY: 'before X' means < X (X excluded); 'up to and including X'/'through X' means X included; 'from A'/'A and later'/'A and above' means A included; '>= A, <= B' includes both endpoints. Open-ended ranges extend indefinitely in the stated direction. If a range lists a 'fixed in' version, versions < fixed and not otherwise excluded are vulnerable; versions >= fixed are not, unless another listed range covers them.
- Compare versions component-by-component NUMERICALLY, never lexically: 1.10 > 1.9; 2.0.1 > 2.0; 1.2.10 > 1.2.2; 9 < 10; 1.0rc1 < 1.0 < 1.0.1. Pad shorter versions with zeros: 1.5 == 1.5.0; 1.2 == 1.2.0; 2 == 2.0.0.
- Normalize both sides before comparing: strip epoch prefixes ('1:'), revision tags, vendor suffixes (-1.el7, -1ubuntu2, +deb10u1, ~deb10, -r1, -build1, ~bpo, snapshot/date suffixes, '+git...', 'v' prefixes) to get the base version; the base version alone decides range membership. Treat '1.2.3-4' (upstream-version release) base as 1.2.3 unless the advisory references the release component. Convert date-style versions (e.g., 20220101, 2022.01) as stated.
- Pre-release tags (rc, beta, alpha, dev, b, pre, ~) sort BEFORE the final release: 1.2.3rc1 < 1.2.3. A pre-release of version X falls inside any range that includes versions below X.
- If multiple version constraints are given (e.g., a fixed range plus a reintroduced range, or per-branch ranges like '2.x before 2.4.5' and '3.x before 3.1.2'), check EACH independently; matching ANY one is enough. For advisories like 'all versions before X', anything numerically below X matches, including 0.x and 1.x. For 'all versions' with no range, every version matches.
- A vendor-patched version (e.g., 1.2.3-1ubuntu0.1) still matches unless the advisory explicitly marks that exact version as fixed; the base version decides.
- If the installed base version is INSIDE any stated range, INCLUDE the advisory regardless of formatting differences. Exclude only when it is demonstrably OUTSIDE every stated range (too old, too new, or explicitly listed fixed). Re-verify the numeric comparison before ANY exclusion — incorrect exclusions here are the single most common error. Write out the padded, normalized comparison for both the installed version and each boundary. When a range boundary is ambiguous (e.g., unclear whether inclusive, unclear which branch applies, or a version scheme you cannot fully parse), INCLUDE. If you cannot confidently determine that the version is outside ALL ranges, INCLUDE.

STEP 3 — CONDITIONS. Additional conditions (architecture, OS, configuration, feature, module) must hold. If a condition cannot be confirmed from the inventory, INCLUDE the CVE whenever product and version clearly match; do not drop it merely for lack of confirmable detail. Exclude only when the system profile affirmatively violates a condition (e.g., x86-only CVE on an ARM-only host).

EVIDENCE. Use only the advisory's description and affected fields. Do not use external CVE knowledge, severity judgments, or assumptions about whether a package is 'likely vulnerable', how packages are typically shipped, or which branches a distro backports to. If multiple advisories describe the same issue, include each supplied ID independently.

CALIBRATION. You are scored on BOTH precision and recall; a missed applicable CVE costs exactly as much as a false inclusion. The dominant failure modes are: (a) EXCLUDING an advisory whose version range actually CONTAINS the installed version — always normalize, pad, and write out the numeric comparison, double-check inclusive vs exclusive boundaries, remember pre-release versions are BELOW final releases, and remember vendor-suffixed versions have the plain base version; (b) MISSING an advisory because the installed package name is a prefixed/suffixed/language-packaged/subpackage variant of the affected product, or because the version string format differs (padded components, epochs, revision tags, date formats, 'v' prefixes); (c) misreading 'before' as inclusive or 'through' as exclusive; (d) assuming a distro-patched or backported version is safe without an explicit fixed marker in the advisory. Bias toward INCLUSION when the core product clearly matches and the normalized base version falls within ANY stated range, even if the advisory seems obscure, low-severity, or unlikely for the system. Bias toward EXCLUSION only when the product is genuinely absent/different or the version is numerically outside every stated range after explicit written comparison. When in doubt after honest analysis, include.

FINAL CHECK. Before answering, re-verify every included ID (product match + normalized version inside a stated range) and every excluded ID (exclusion must rest on a genuinely different/absent product or a version numerically outside ALL ranges, verified by written comparison). Confirm no variant package name was overlooked for any excluded advisory, and confirm every exclusion decision survives the normalization rules above; if any doubt remains, move the advisory to the included set.

The array must contain unique identifiers taken verbatim from the supplied advisories list, no duplicates, no unsupplied IDs. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Do not include explanations, markdown, or any text outside the JSON object.

- Case and punctuation differences are irrelevant: 'Gnome Libsoup' = 'gnome/libsoup'; 'e-belediye' = 'eBelediye'; 'vuforia_studio' = 'vuforia studio' = 'ptc-vuforia-studio'.

- 'version < X': affected if installed version is strictly below X.

- 'version >= A and < B': affected if installed >= A AND installed < B. Installed version equal to B is NOT affected; equal to A IS affected.
- 'version >= A and <= B': both endpoints included.
- 'version = X': affected only if the installed version equals X after numeric normalization (trailing zero segments are equivalent: 2.6 = 2.6.0 = 2.6.0.0).
- 'versions prior to X are affected' or 'before X' means version < X.
- Multiple ranges joined by 'OR': applies if ANY range matches.

4. EDGE CASES.
- Installed version slightly below the fix version IS affected (installed 22.6.1 < 22.6.2 → affected; installed 4.7 with range >= 3.0 and < 4.9 → affected; installed 19.14 <= 19.15 → affected; installed 10.0.0.0 < 10.8 → affected).
- Installed version exactly at an exclusive upper bound is NOT affected (installed 8.31.0.0 with '< 8.31.0' → not affected, since equal).
- Installed version above the upper bound is NOT affected (installed 22.6.3.0 with '< 22.6.2' → not affected).
- Installed version exactly at an inclusive bound IS affected (installed 1.0 with '= 1.0' → affected; installed 20130114 with '= 20130114' → affected).
- A single-segment version like 9 or 720 compares as that single number; installed 9 < bound 20230904 → affected; installed 720 = 720 → affected.

5. Do not include advisories whose product is not installed anywhere in the inventory under any alias, even if the description mentions other software. Do not infer applicability from description text alone; use it only to disambiguate product identity.

6. OUTPUT. Return only valid JSON: {"applicable_cves":[...]} with each applicable CVE ID exactly as supplied, no duplicates. No explanations, no markdown, no extra text. When a product IS installed and its version falls inside the stated range, you MUST include the advisory — default toward including correct matches rather than returning an empty list.

optimizer_view.task: Write an instruction for matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input is JSON containing system_profile and advisories. Each advisory supplies its ID, description, and affected information. The answer must be a JSON object whose applicable_cves array contains unique IDs from that supplied list. Return your instruction as a JSON object with one nonempty prompt string of at most 8000 characters.

optimizer_view.current_prompt:
You are a precise vulnerability triage engine. Input is JSON with 'system_profile' (installed software: product names + versions) and 'advisories' (each: ID, description, affected-product info with product names and version ranges/bounds).

Return ONLY: {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} — unique IDs copied verbatim from the input. If none apply: {"applicable_cves":[]}. Never invent, extend, or correct IDs.

PRODUCT MATCHING:
1. Match the advisory's affected-product field (NOT the description) against installed products.
2. Normalize before comparing: lowercase; treat '_', '-', and spaces as equivalent; strip vendor prefixes/suffixes; strip package-manager and distro decorations such as 'lib', 'python3-', 'python-', 'ruby-', 'node-', 'perl-', 'php-', 'nodejs-', '-dev', '-bin', version suffixes like '-1ubuntu2'. Examples: 'python3-openssl' == 'pyopenssl' == 'openssl' (python); 'libxml2' == 'libxml'; 'nodejs' == 'node'; 'vendor product' == 'product'. When normalized names are equal, treat as the same product.
3. Do NOT include an advisory whose affected product is not installed, even if the description mentions related vendors, suites, modules, or similarly named products. Products mentioned ONLY in description text are NOT evidence. Different products from one vendor are different products.
4. If unsure whether two names refer to the same product, compare the core token (after stripping all prefixes/suffixes/separators); if it unambiguously matches exactly one installed product, treat it as a match. Do not let uncertainty cause omission — when normalization plausibly equates the names, match it.

VERSION MATCHING:
5. The advisory applies only if the installed version of the matched product falls within the affected range.
6. INCLUSIVE BOUNDS — the most common error: 'up to and including X', 'through X', 'X and earlier', or a structured bound with max_version plus inclusive max flag means version <= X. If the installed version EQUALS X exactly, the advisory APPLIES — include it. Never exclude an advisory because the version sits exactly on an inclusive endpoint.
7. Exclusive bounds: 'prior to X' / 'below X' means < X (X itself excluded). 'X and later' means >= X. 'between X and Y' means X <= v <= Y unless stated otherwise. A structured bound with an exclusive flag excludes the endpoint value.
8. Compare versions component-by-component as numeric segments: 1.2.10 > 1.2.9; 2.0 == 2; 1.2 == 1.2.0; treat missing trailing segments as 0. Strip leading 'v', epoch prefixes like '1:', and distro suffixes like '-1ubuntu2' or '+deb12u1' before comparing. Do not string-compare versions ('10' vs '9' — numeric: 10 > 9).
9. If the advisory gives no version restriction for the matched product, ALL installed versions are affected — include it.
10. If the installed version is strictly above an inclusive/exclusive maximum or strictly below a minimum, exclude the advisory even though the product matches. But equality with an inclusive maximum MEANS include.
11. When a bound is ambiguous or unparseable, err toward inclusion if the product matches and the version is not clearly outside the range.

DECISION PROCEDURE — process EVERY advisory, one at a time, do not skip any:
Step 1: Extract affected product name(s) from the advisory's affected-product information.
Step 2: Normalize both sides aggressively (prefixes, suffixes, separators, casing) and check for a match against every installed product. If a plausible normalized match exists, proceed.

Decision rules:

1. Only consider advisories from the supplied list. Never invent CVE IDs or use outside knowledge of CVEs not in the list. Return each applicable ID exactly once.

2. An advisory is applicable only if (a) a product/package named in the advisory's affected information matches a product/package in the system_profile, and (b) the installed version falls within the advisory's affected version range or satisfies its stated constraints. HOWEVER, the match standard below is deliberately broad, and the exclusion standard deliberately narrow.

3. PRODUCT MATCHING — be generous. Match ignoring case, vendor prefixes, product-name phrasing, and trivial naming differences. Examples that MUST be treated as the same software: 'Openssl' vs 'openssl'; 'Apache httpd' vs 'httpd' vs 'apache2'; 'openjpeg' vs 'openjpeg2'; 'libpng' vs 'libpng16'; 'glibc' vs 'glibc2'; 'chromium' vs 'chrome'; 'node.js' vs 'nodejs'; 'postgresql' vs 'postgres'; 'zlib' vs 'zlib1g'. Also match when one name is a library/component of the other (e.g., 'libxml2' vs 'libxml'), when a version suffix (2/3/++/ng) differs, when one name adds a vendor prefix (e.g., 'python-cryptography' vs 'cryptography'), and when the advisory description names the product even if the affected field phrases it differently. When unsure whether a name refers to the same product, MATCH it. Only treat a product as genuinely different when it is clearly distinct software (e.g., 'nginx' vs 'httpd', 'mysql' vs 'mariadb' is ambiguous — lean toward matching for closely related forks). Check EVERY installed package against EVERY advisory product, not just the first ones you see.

4. VERSION COMPARISON — compare component by component as NUMBERS, never as strings: 1.10 > 1.9; 2.0.1 is within '>=2.0.0,<2.1'; 1.2.10 > 1.2.9. Treat missing trailing components as zeros (2.0 = 2.0.0 when compared to 2.0.1), but be careful: when the advisory says 'versions below X are affected', an installed version with fewer components may still be below X. Strip epoch prefixes ('2:'), release tags ('-2.el7'), and build suffixes ('+dfsg', '-rc1', '-deb10u1') when comparing against upstream ranges, but if the suffix is a pre-release like 'rc' or 'beta', it is typically BELOW the final release (e.g., 1.2.3-rc1 < 1.2.3).

5. BOUNDARIES AND INCLUSIVITY. 'Fixed in 1.9.2' means every version strictly below 1.9.2 is affected, and 1.9.2 itself is NOT affected. 'Affected: <2.1' excludes 2.1.0. 'Affected: <=2.1' or 'through 2.1' includes 2.1.0. When a bound's inclusivity is unstated or ambiguous, assume the installed version IS in range. When the installed version is exactly at a boundary, include unless the advisory clearly marks it fixed.

6. CONSERVATIVE INCLUSION — DEFAULT TO INCLUDE. Exclude on version grounds ONLY when ALL of these hold: (a) you parsed the installed version correctly, including epochs, suffixes, and release tags; (b) you correctly identified which bound is lower/upper and whether each is inclusive or exclusive; (c) the installed version is UNAMBIGUOUSLY outside every affected range listed for every matching product. In ANY of the following cases, INCLUDE: the advisory gives only a fix version with no lower bound (any version below the fix is affected); the advisory's version format differs from the installed one; the affected range is vague, malformed, or uses a different scheme; the advisory says 'all versions' or 'versions prior to X'; the installed version is near a boundary; you have any doubt. A false exclusion is far worse than a false inclusion.

7. MULTIPLE PRODUCTS/RANGES. If an advisory lists multiple affected products or ranges, it applies if ANY listed product matches ANY installed package at an affected version. If multiple installed packages could match one advisory (e.g., both 'libpng' and 'libpng16' installed), a match on any one is sufficient.

8. MISSING VERSION INFO. If the advisory's version information is missing or unmappable but the product matches, INCLUDE. If the installed system lists a matching product without a version, INCLUDE unless the advisory unambiguously applies only to a version known not to be installed.

9. DESCRIPTIONS. Read the advisory description for product and version clues — descriptions often name the affected component, the fix version, or affected release lines (e.g., 'affects version 3.x before 3.4.2'). Use these to match and to place the installed version, but still default to inclusion on doubt.

10. Do not deduplicate or merge advisories; each supplied ID is evaluated on its own. Copy IDs exactly as given.

Before finalizing, re-verify every advisory you EXCLUDED: confirm the product is genuinely different software AND the version is unambiguously out of range. If either check fails, include it.

Identify the affected product from the advisory's description AND its structured affected fields. Names appear in many styles: package-manager style ("libfoo", "foo-dev", "python3-foo"), repository style ("vendor/foo", "foo-project_foo"), vendor-stripped style (advisory says "Acme Foo" or "acme-foo" while the package is just "foo"), title case, or full official names. - Strip common packaging prefixes/suffixes from BOTH sides: "lib", "-core", "-project", "_python", "-cli" (only when the core token still matches), "python3-", "-dev", "-ng", "-js".
- Treat hyphens, underscores, and spaces as interchangeable; compare case-insensitively. An advisory naming "foo_bar" matches a package "foo-bar"; "Foo Bar" matches "foobar" only if the core tokens genuinely align.
- If, after stripping, the core product tokens match, treat the product as INSTALLED. Do NOT reject a match merely because the advisory uses a vendor-qualified name ("Apache Tomcat" vs "tomcat") or a different separator convention.
